title: Beyond Reconstruction: A Unified Framework for Trustworthy and Explainable EEG Artifact Removal Evaluation
summary: Deep-learning methods have achieved strong performance in EEG artifact removal, but evaluation remains dominated by reconstruction metrics such as error, correlation, and signal-to-noise ratio. Although these metrics assess similarity to clean EEG, they do not establish whether models effectively suppress artifacts, preserve neural activity, or provide reliable explanations. To address these limitations, we propose TriX-EEG, a three-level framework for trustworthy and explainable EEG artifact removal. Level 1, Signal Validity (SV), evaluates reconstruction quality and neural band-power preservation. Level 2, Removal Faithfulness (RF), assesses the removed component through artifact error and residual artifact/neural leakage. Level 3, Explanation Reliability (ER), examines model behavior through temporal alignment, causal relevance, and stability. We evaluate TriX-EEG using nine published neural denoisers across three public benchmarks derived from EEGDenoiseNet and the PhysioNet Motion Artifact Contaminated EEG Dataset, covering EOG, EMG, and motion artifacts. Results show that reconstruction metrics alone are insufficient for trustworthy denoiser assessment: RF complements it by revealing whether errors stem from residual artifact or suppressed neural activity, while ER captures distinct aspects of explanation behavior, supporting joint evaluation of three aspects within a unified framework rather than reliance on any single factor. External validation on an independent EEG/EOG dataset and the BCI Competition IV-2a motor-imagery dataset further demonstrates broadly consistent rankings under dataset shift. Higher-ranked denoisers generally preserve more task-relevant information or cause less downstream performance degradation. Overall, TriX-EEG provides a comprehensive basis for EEG denoiser assessment, encouraging models that are not only accurate but also faithful and explainable.

title: The Impact of Scenario Representation in Scenario-based Optimization Certification
summary: Scenario-based optimization provides finite-sample guarantees for decisions constructed from sampled uncertainty, but its certification procedures can be sensitive to how those samples are represented. We investigate this sensitivity under lossless scenario regrouping, which preserves the sampled information, feasible region, optimizer, and primitive violation probability. For an equal-allocation support-subsample certificate, we derive the distortion factor \(k^2(1-ε)^{k-1}\), establish certification reversals between equivalent representations, and provide sufficient conditions for acceptance dominance under nested coarsening. We further apply nondegeneracy-free Wait-and-Judge theory to coordinatewise scenario envelopes, enabling stronger certification directly from the primitive observations. In paired scenario-MPC experiments, exact regrouping increases certification availability from 318 to 471 of 480 attempts without changing the samples, numerical proposals, or requiring any reduction in witness cardinality. Primitive Wait-and-Judge certification accepts the same 471 attempts without regrouping. These results demonstrate that apparent scenario sample-efficiency gains can arise from certificate accounting rather than additional information or reduced decision risk.

title: Mechanism Design and Active Systems Theory: 60 Years of Parallel Development
summary: The survey compares two research traditions within the mathematical theory of designing the rules of interaction (mechanisms) for purposeful participants: mechanism design, together with contract theory and implementation theory, and the theory of active systems created by V.N. Burkov and developed into the theory of control in organizations (TCO) by D.A. Novikov's school; the main results of Yu.B. Germeier's school and of the domestic schools adjacent to active systems theory (AST) are covered as well. The problem statements and principal results of 2006-2026 are presented: for mechanism design (MD) - robust and dynamic mechanism design, multidimensional screening, information design, simplicity of mechanisms and credibility of the designer, market design, algorithmic and learning-based design, mechanisms for AI agents, and robust, relational, dynamic and algorithmic contracts; for AST and TCO - a general typology of control, strategy-proof and incentive-compatible planning mechanisms, decomposition of the agents' game, systems with distributed control and coalitional interaction, reflexive games and informational control, control of staff and structure, dynamic active systems, and project management. A correspondence between the classical results is established (the fair play principle and the revelation principle, the serial resource allocation mechanism and the uniform rule, active expertise mechanisms and generalized median schemes, quasi-compensatory incentive schemes and contracts under observable actions), and priorities are delineated by uniform rules; the areas where the two traditions diverge are identified, as are the dimensions of the problem (staff, structure, institutions, awareness, agents' beliefs) covered only by TCO.

title: Tie-Line Scheduling Using Real-Time Contraction Metrics: Hierarchical Reachable Sets for Multi-Area Inverter-Dominated Grids
summary: Managing transmission congestion in multi-area power grids dominated by inverter-based resources (IBRs) requires bridging a severe timescale and modeling divide. Supervisory congestion optimizers -- such as Online Feedback Optimization (OFO) and two-tiered differentiable Model Predictive Control (MPC) -- rely on linearized, convex algebraic grid approximations that cannot guarantee dynamic stability during sub-second converter transients. Conversely, fast distributed consensus schemes like Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) depend on convex plant assumptions and iterative message exchanges that lag behind rapid tie-line surges. This paper replaces convex ADMM emergency consensus with a Distributed Nonlinear Separable Control Contraction Metric (SCCM) architecture spanning three nested tiers: the Device layer, the Area layer, and the Grid tie-line layer. By pairing online Prediction Error Method and Moving Horizon Estimation (PEM-MHE) parameter tracking with offline convex Linear Matrix Inequality (LMI) synthesis, the controller executes a closed-form nonlinear feedback law online without solving real-time optimization problems. We derive the Pontryagin attainable (reachable) ellipsoids for each layer, prove hierarchical tube containment via Schur-complement matrix inequalities, and project the certified Grid reachable tube through Power Transfer Distribution Factors (PTDFs) to supply guaranteed safe thermal limits to the supervisory coordinator. Validation on modified IEEE 39-bus (100% IBR, zero synchronous generators) and 3-area IEEE 118-bus systems demonstrates an 82.8% reduction in cumulative tie-line thermal overload while maintaining strict exponential contraction ($λ_{\max} \le -2.43$) even under a 3 s communication blackout.

title: Kernel Tuning for the HSIC-Based Global Sensitivity Analysis of High-Dimensional Models
summary: We consider global sensitivity analysis of models with high-dimensional input parameters using HSIC-based indices. The numerical estimation of these kernel-based indices is known to be challenging for such models. Without proper kernel tuning, the standard estimator for the HSIC can become unstable and break down. Focusing on models with independent parameters, we introduce a dimension-aware bandwidth formula and provide theoretical analysis justifying the proposed approach. In particular, we show that unless kernel bandwidth parameters explicitly scale with the input dimension, the corresponding sensitivity indices return uninformative rankings of parameter influence. Further, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed scaling strategy on linear and nonlinear test problems, including models with correlated inputs.

title: A Systematic Survey of Decompilation: Mapping Classical and Machine-Learning Approaches
summary: Context: Decompilers reconstruct source-level code from compiled binaries, and analysts rely on them whenever source code is unavailable. Many recent studies apply machine learning (ML), including large language models, to parts of this task. From the primary literature alone, it is unclear where these methods sit in the classical decompilation pipeline and how well their claims are supported. Objectives: We map decompilation research onto a pipeline-centered taxonomy and ask two questions: where classical, ML-trained, and ML-prompted approaches are positioned (RQ1), and how ML-based studies vary in technical design and evaluation evidence (RQ2). Methods: We surveyed 405 decompilation studies from 1973 to 2026, collected through database search and citation tracing. We classified 394 primary studies into eight pipeline stages and two complementary categories. For the 116 ML-based studies that propose or modify decompilation methods, we extracted the model-use strategy, reusable backbones, target platform, and the evidence behind each evaluation. Results: Classical techniques still dominate front-end recovery, IR lifting, and control-flow structuring (277 of 394 primary studies are classical). ML-based work (117 studies) clusters instead around symbol and name recovery, output refinement, and end-to-end translation. Type recovery is the clearest mixed region. Most ML-based studies target native binaries (97 of 116), and most evidence is item-level matching against references (89 of 116); execution-based tests, human or LLM judgment, and downstream-task evidence are much rarer. Conclusion: ML has not displaced the classical pipeline. It has been taken up where a recovered artifact can be posed as a prediction, translation, or refinement problem, and reported gains only make sense when read against the pipeline position and the evidence used to support them.

title: Who Gets the Grid Capacity? Allocating Dynamic Access Among Multiple Virtual Power Plants
summary: Virtual power plants (VPPs) trade in the same wholesale market and share distribution lines and transformers, and uncoordinated, profit-maximizing VPPs can push a shared transformer past its thermal limit or drive a feeder voltage out of band. The utility, which only observes the front-of-the-meter net injection at each bus, must keep the network safe from that net injection alone. We allocate a 24-hour active and reactive operating envelope to each VPP by a Benders decomposition: the utility sets a trial envelope, each VPP solves its private convex portfolio problem, and the returned value and dual gradient become supporting cuts that rebuild its value function while its schedule, state, and cost stay private. The envelope carries the transformer's thermal state across hours, bounds a joint conditional value-at-risk over forecast uncertainty, and is re-optimized each hour with the current hour committed. On a reduced IEEE-13 feeder with real load and prices, an active-power-only implementation lowers the transformer's peak-temperature CVaR from 254 to 97\,$^\circ$C at a 28\% value give-up and holds the transformer below its limit where nameplate access breaches it.

title: When Is Membership Graded? Identifiability and Resolution Limits of a Graded Gaussian Mixture Model
summary: Mixed-membership models describe each unit as a graded blend of latent types. Before the blend is interpreted, the data should be able to rule out the simpler story in which every unit belongs to a single type. We ask when they can, in a scalar graded Gaussian mixture model, in which each observation is a Beta-weighted convex combination of independent Gaussian draws from two types, the mechanism behind functional mixed-membership models and the normal compositional model. The model is identifiable, unequal variances included, but the identifying information sits in the far tails of the marginal. For the symmetric model we give a closed-form hard-membership mixture that matches the graded marginal in five cumulants, and a Le Cam bound turns it into a certified sample size below which no test separates graded from hard membership with summed error under one half. The threshold is governed by the concentration $c$ relative to $c_0\approx d^2$, where $d$ is the type half-separation in within-type standard deviations. At $d=3$ it is about 2,600 observations at $c=3$ and 77,000 at $c=6$. Most of the difficulty comes from learning $c$. On 100 simulated datasets with graded membership, a correctly specified posterior under the default priors of a published Bayesian sampler for this model class reports hard membership every time, a weak prior gives intervals for the concentration spanning orders of magnitude, and the sampler's own answers depend on where it starts.

title: Exploring Test Smells Across Programming Languages: A Systematic Mapping Study
summary: Tests are essential for ensuring code quality in software development. However, poor implementation practices can compromise the maintainability and evolution of test code, leading to additional costs and effort. These practices, known as test smells, have been the focus of numerous studies that expanded the catalog of known test smells. Despite this progress, little attention has been given to examining test smells from the perspective of programming languages, particularly their relationship with specific languages or test frameworks. As a result, researchers and practitioners have proposed various approaches and tools to detect and refactor the same test smells across different languages. In this work, we address this gap by analyzing test smells in the literature from a programming language perspective. We conducted a systematic mapping study, gathering data from papers published up to August 2025, examining 117 papers. We identified the most prevalent languages and frameworks associated with test smells, the most common test smells in each language, refactorings for addressing test smells, datasets of test smells, the criticality of specific test smells, and a collection of tools to detect or refactor test smells for various languages and frameworks. Our results show that while many test smells have been addressed, research remains limited to a few languages and frameworks. We also found datasets and detection/refactoring tools for some languages and analyzed the criticality of frequently mentioned test smells. This study highlights the need to expand research to more languages and develop more universal solutions.

title: Emerging Vertical Power Delivery in AI Data Centers: Challenges and Solutions
comment: 29 pages, 24 figures. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) workloads is increasing power demand in AI data centers, and processor current is projected to reach 2000 A and beyond. This trend is exposing the limitations of lateral power delivery (LPD) to processors and has motivated growing interest in vertical power delivery (VPD). This paper reviews the power delivery network (PDN) of AI data centers and the upcoming transition from LPD to VPD. First, the 800 VDC power delivery architecture, the impedance behavior of the PDN, and the limitations of LPD are discussed. Then, VPD implementation approaches, reported converter designs, and packaging technologies are examined, together with integrated voltage regulators (IVRs) and embedded passive components. In addition, power integrity simulations are presented to compare regulator and plane positions, from which a set of PDN design guidelines is derived. The results show that moving a voltage regulator module (VRM) from 50 mm away to directly below the die reduces the loop inductance by nearly half. In a complete PDN, this relocation lowers the low-frequency anti-resonant peak, whereas the mid- and high-frequency impedance depends on the decoupling stages and the position of the power and ground planes. This paper also shows that achieving practical VPD remains closely tied to challenges such as regulator height, passive-component embedding, and thermal management.

title: Simultaneous analysis of approximate leave-one-out cross-validation and mean-field inference II: General convex penalties
comment: Part I is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.02624. Lean files can be found in the arXiv ancillary files
summary:
For smooth penalties and group Lasso, analyzed approximate leave-one-out (ALO) cross-validation by comparing its weights with the trace correction used in mean-field inference. For a $C^2$ penalty $R$, the matrix entering these corrections is $A=[\nabla^2R(\widehat b)+X^TDX]^{-1}$, where $\widehat b$ is the full-data estimator and $D$ is the diagonal matrix of fitted loss curvatures; for group Lasso, the penalty and loss curvatures are first restricted to the active support before taking the pseudoinverse.
  The obstacle to extending this argument to general convex penalties was the lack of an explicit formula for the matrix $A$ entering these corrections. For every finite-valued strongly convex penalty, we construct such a matrix from ordinary derivatives of the penalty response at the observed subgradient. Its projection--pseudoinverse formula separates the response space and penalty curvature, fixed by conditioning, from the explicit design dependence. This supplies the missing ingredient to extend the probabilistic argument of Part~I. The construction recovers the inverse Hessian for smooth penalties and the active-group inverse for group Lasso, including inactive boundary groups.
  In the proportional regime, for Gaussian designs with general positive-definite covariance and covariance-scaled strong convexity, we obtain unconditional bounds comparing both ALO and mean-field predictions with exact leave-one-out predictions in regression and single-index models. The expected average squared prediction error is $O(n^{-1})$, and the expected absolute criterion error is $O(n^{-1/2})$, under bounded, 1-Lipschitz loss scores and suitable test functions. The matrix and ALO weights use only observed data; the mean-field correction additionally uses the design covariance. The construction, recovery identities and statistical guarantees are formalized in Lean~4.

title: Does Your Agent Need to Know Its Budget? A Placebo-Controlled Experiment on LLM Coding Agents
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Study archive (frozen protocol, per-run logs, and analysis code) to be deposited in a DOI-issuing repository
summary: Organizations deploying autonomous coding agents impose token budgets, yet the causal effects of a budget, and of telling the agent about it, are unmeasured. We conduct a placebo-controlled factorial experiment under a frozen, timestamped protocol, crossing budget enforcement with budget disclosure on two executable program-repair benchmarks (5,835 runs, two open models, three cap levels). Enforcing a calibrated cap reduced task resolution by 20.0 percentage points while reducing tokens per resolved task roughly twelvefold. Disclosing the enforced budget never helped: the placebo-controlled risk difference was -2.8 pp (95% CI [-6.2, +0.7]) at the medium cap and -4.2 pp ([-8.1, -0.2], nominally significant, unadjusted) at the tight cap, with every prompt wording and per-turn feedback variant far below the 10-point effect size of interest. Observed run-to-run outcome variance was roughly 1.5x the uncapped level under caps, though part of this reflects resolution rates moving nearer one half. These results make budget governance for coding agents an enforcement-design problem: no communication variant produced an effect beyond that of an unrelated sentence, which itself raised resolution by 7.2 pp (95% CI [+4.0, +10.5]) over silent enforcement, a sentence effect that only a placebo control removes.

title: First-Order Model-Free Policy Gradient for Undiscounted LQR with Global Optimality and Convergence Guarantees
summary: We provide a first-order model-free policy gradient (PG) framework for learning undiscounted infinite-horizon linear quadratic regulator (LQR) policies with global optimality and convergence guarantees. We first construct a stochastic wrapper policy class parameterized by the LQR gain to enable exploration around a deterministic linear control law. We analyze the additional cost induced by exploration over infinite-horizon, and establish a weak gradient dominance condition that characterizes global optimality under exploration. We then construct a model-free first-order PG algorithm using sampled trajectory information, without identifying the dynamics or approximating a value function. Finally, we establish finite-time convergence guarantees, providing the sufficient number of samples required for near-global optimality with our proposed PG algorithms.

title: A δ-adjusted Method for Tipping Point Sensitivity Analysis for a Binary Outcome with Missing Values
summary: Missing data remain a persistent challenge in clinical trials despite preventive efforts. Handling missing data in clinical trials requires not only a primary analysis but also sensitivity analyses, as the underlying missingness assumptions are difficult to verify. The δ-adjusted analysis, which assesses the robustness of primary results by adding a sensitivity parameter δ for one or both treatment groups, has been widely used for continuous outcomes. Then, a set of tipping points which flip the significance of the primary analysis can be identified. However, there is no corresponding δ-adjusted method for binary variables. In this article, we propose a δ-adjusted method for binary variables that addresses this gap. This method assesses robustness by adding a sensitivity parameter to the logit function of the estimated response probability under the primary imputation approach and shares the same property as the δ-adjusted method for continuous variables. We applied this method to a clinical trial evaluating the treatment effect of tirzepatide 15 mg versus 5 mg on a composite binary endpoint. This method provides a principled sensitivity analysis framework for binary endpoints with broad applicability in clinical trials.

title: Wrong yet Confident: Automated Detection of Silent Failures in Location-Dependent Software
summary: We report an experience paper applying round-trip offset---an automated testing oracle for location-dependent software---at deployment scale across 32,019 GPS delivery transactions, corresponding to 24,501 unique coordinates, from a single USDA COVID-19 food assistance deployment in Bayamón, Puerto Rico. The oracle tests each geocoder's implicit spatial accuracy claim by measuring the deviation between an input coordinate and the coordinate recovered after reverse-then-forward geocoding, without requiring manual labeling of correctness. We evaluated one community-contributed and two commercial geocoders against this operationally validated corpus. The experience surfaces two distinct failure classes, which we report with their respective denominators because they are not comparable quantities. First, 2,441 of the 24,501 unique coordinates (10.0%) are invisible to all three platforms: an acknowledged failure with no resolution, and a property of the corpus rather than of any one geocoder. Second, and platform-specific: 10.0% of the 13,221 coordinates Google resolves to a civic address exhibit round-trip offsets exceeding 2~km---5.4% of the full corpus---returned with no error signal, against 0.5% for the second commercial platform and 0.04% for the community geocoder. Round-trip offset detects all large-offset failures observed in this dataset while standard resolution-rate evaluation detects none. We document an eight-mode fault taxonomy, a structured comparison of detection methods, and concrete lessons for integrating automated geocoder verification into CI/CD pipelines. The key lesson: resolution rate measures availability; round-trip offset measures correctness. In non-standard addressing environments these two metrics select for opposite behaviors, and only the latter catches the failures that matter for autonomous action.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning with Hard Constraints: Policy Gradient Methods with Intersample Guarantees
summary: We develop a policy-gradient (PG) reinforcement learning (RL) framework with hard inter-sample control barrier function (CBF)-based safety constraints for nonlinear sampled-data systems. We first design a class of stochastic policies with support truncated to sampling-period-dependent safe control sets, that guarantee safety-by-construction at sampling instants. We then propose a model-free PG algorithm that searches over the class of safe-by-design policies and establish sufficient conditions on sampling-period such that any action sampled from safe control sets remains safe throughout the sampling interval, providing inter-sample guarantees. We further establish finite-time convergence and sample complexity guarantees for the proposed PG algorithm and characterize its global optimality under gradient dominance. Finally, we illustrate inter-sample safety guarantees on a safe quadrotor navigation environment.

title: Robust Decision Curve Analysis for Survival Risk Prediction Models in the Presence of Informative Censoring
comment: 21 pages, 4 figures; Abdollah Safari and Tae Yoon Lee equally contributed
summary: Decision curve analysis (DCA) is recommended for evaluating the clinical utility of prediction models by quantifying net benefit (NB). Conventional NB estimators for survival outcomes rely on the assumption that censoring is non-informative, potentially yielding biased estimates and misleading decisions when this assumption is violated. We propose a robust estimator of survival NB using conditional inverse probability of censoring weighting (CIPCW). In simulation studies, we compared its performance against the conventional approach across censoring mechanisms, censoring model specifications, censoring rates, and decision thresholds, in terms of relative bias, relative root mean squared error (RMSE), and 90% confidence interval coverage. Under non-informative censoring, both estimators performed comparably, with relative bias below 1% and coverage close to the nominal level. Under informative censoring, conventional estimators underestimated the true NB by up to 58% with coverage as low as 1%, whereas the CIPCW estimator had a relative bias of at most 4%, coverage of at least 78% and consistently lower relative RMSE. As a case study, we illustrated its use in validating a breast cancer recurrence-free survival model to guide intensified adjuvant therapy in the German Breast Cancer Study Group (GBSG) cohort. Using the model was the best strategy at some clinically relevant thresholds, but accounting for potential informative censoring changed the best strategy to treating all patients, showing that informative censoring can change the conclusions drawn from DCA. When censoring may be informative, we recommend CIPCW-based NB estimation in DCA for survival outcomes.

title: Revision-Consistent Code Context for Agents That Edit Their Environment
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures. Source code and reproducibility artifacts are available at https://github.com/mengshi02/codetrip
summary:
Editing agents query repositories while simultaneously changing them. Source content, symbols, graph relations, and retrieval state may be maintained by different stores and refreshed at different times. During an update, a successful query can therefore combine facts that never belonged to the same repository state. We call this condition mixed-revision code context.
  This paper proposes an Agent-visible complete-revision publication contract for composite code-intelligence queries. Before a query-visible publication point, a service must wait, report unavailability, or serve a complete old revision; after that point, it serves the complete new revision. The contract requires a shared version identity and publication boundary across every view returned in one response.
  We instantiate the method in Codetrip, whose brief operation joins source, symbol, and graph facts. In a controlled comparison on frozen Gin v1.12.0, live-source composition produced two unsafe responses in 150 update trials, whereas complete-revision publication produced none under the same five edit scenarios. We further implement journaled, idempotent publication and terminate the real MCP process at five durable boundaries. All 300 evaluable recovery trials on frozen Gin and Cobra returned complete-new context equivalent to a clean full rebuild, with median restart-to-context latency of 77--131 ms. In a separate rename probe, mixed context occurred in 0/30 Codetrip trials and 30/30 trials for both CodeGraph and codebase-memory-mcp before clean-full-equivalent convergence.
  The contribution is an Agent-facing safety contract, implementation pattern, and measurement protocol for joining live repository bytes with asynchronously derived facts. Every successful composite response consequently has a testable repository-state meaning, including after interruption.

title: PS-HalluBench: Taxonomy-Driven Benchmarking of LLM Hallucinations in Power Systems
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for power-system applications, yet their reliability in engineering analysis remains uncertain. We introduce PS-HalluBench, a manually constructed benchmark of 200 questions that evaluates hallucination-related failures across five power-system task categories: numerical reasoning, network topology, constraint verification, false-premise acceptance, and abstention. We evaluate ten LLMs over the benchmark, yielding 39.35\% overall correctness, with constraint verification achieving only 21.75\%, and highlighting persistent difficulties in engineering reasoning. We further investigate engineering-grounded reasoning through numerical solver support and verified network information both of which show significant performance improvement. The findings reveal important limitations of standalone LLM reasoning and motivate integrating LLMs with verified engineering tools for reliable power-system analysis.

title: Modeling Document and Section Hierarchies in Embedding Space
summary: Embedded topic models integrate word embeddings into the topic generation process, producing coherent topics and robust performance on large vocabularies. However, each document is represented by a single topic distribution, ignoring its internal structure. Many real world collections, including legal documents, company and government reports, and online discussion forums, exhibit hierarchical organization in which documents consist of multiple sections that often address distinct subtopics. We introduce the Hierarchical Embedded Topic Model (hETM), a structured topic model that couples the topic distribution of a document and those of its sections through a hierarchical prior in the embedding space. We derive an amortized variational inference procedure for hETM and evaluate it on structured collections from each of these domains. Experimental results show that hETM achieves the lowest or near-lowest held-out perplexity among flat and hierarchical topic model baselines, along with comparable or higher topic quality. It also performs strongly on a downstream clustering task, achieving the best clustering performance on most of the collections.

title: A Chain-of-Thought Prompt Engineering Framework for Automated Technical Specification Generation in Enterprise Integration: A Real-World Case Study
summary: Technical Specification Documents (TSDs) translate functional requirements into implementable designs and are mandatory artifacts in governed Enterprise Application Integration (EAI) programs, yet their production remains a manual, expertise-intensive bottleneck. Large Language Models (LLMs) have been studied extensively for code generation, but long-form, template-governed engineering documents remain comparatively unexplored. This paper reports an industrial case study, conducted during a migration of more than 250 enterprise integrations to Microsoft Azure Integration Services at a large Australian wholesale distributor, that introduces a chain-of-thought prompt-engineering framework for automated TSD generation using GitHub Copilot. The framework combines a two-phase generation architecture that grounds the model in the functional specification, organizational standards, and the approved template; a six-stage prompting pipeline with human validation checkpoints; and Prompt-as-a-Code, under which prompts are version-controlled and reviewed as engineering artifacts. Applied to a stratified sample of fifteen production interfaces, the framework reduced TSD authoring effort from 793 to 300 person-hours, a 62.2% pooled reduction and a 64.0% mean per-document reduction (Wilcoxon signed-rank, n = 15, p < 0.001), at 74.3% reviewer-assessed accuracy and 3.7/5 developer satisfaction. Benefits degrade monotonically with interface complexity: between the simplest and most complex bands, effort reduction falls from 70.6% to 58.9% and accuracy from 91% to 62.5%, and the residual human effort concentrates in diagrams, sequence flows, and cross-system integration content. We additionally report comparative observations of GPT-4.1/5 and Claude Sonnet 4, as well as Copilot's Ask and Agent interaction modes, offering reusable, practice-grounded guidance for enterprise settings.

title: An Explainable Agentic AI Framework for Distribution System Load Restoration
summary: Distribution system load restoration is a sequential decision-making problem in which restoration actions must maximize served load, prioritize critical loads, and preserve power-flow feasibility. This paper proposes an explainable agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework for distribution system load restoration. The proposed framework uses multiple large language model (LLM) agents for planner guidance, strategic plan generation, decision arbitration, memory-based feedback, and explanation generation. Unlike unconstrained LLM-based control, the proposed method restricts agent decisions to feasible restoration actions and evaluates all candidate plans using deterministic AC power-flow feasibility checks. The framework is evaluated on IEEE 33-bus and 69-bus distribution feeders, as well as a larger IEEE 118-bus test case, and compared against reinforcement learning and planning baselines. The results show that the proposed agentic framework achieves better restoration performance while producing structured explanations for operator-facing decision support. A direct comparison with a Single-LLM-Agent baseline further shows that the proposed multi-agent decomposition improves weighted restored load and critical-load recovery compared with a monolithic LLM decision structure.

title: Deep Learning Models for Fractional Option Pricing
summary: This paper investigates whether neural networks can infer fractional option prices and the Hurst parameter directly from sequences of fractional Gaussian returns, without separately estimating the latent parameters for each new sequence. Feedforward neural networks (FNNs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are trained to jointly predict European call prices, put prices, and the Hurst parameter from 252-return sequences. A controlled simulation varies the total sample size from 5,000 to 500,000 sequences and evaluates point prediction, empirical residual-based prediction intervals, and computational performance. The neural-network models are also compared on a common simulated test set with Bayesian joint estimation and exact Gaussian maximum likelihood estimation. In that four-method comparison, the LSTM achieves the lowest Hurst-parameter root mean squared error (0.033) and option-price root mean squared error (1.305). After training, neural-network predictions are substantially faster than repeated parameter estimation, although the methods quantify uncertainty in different ways. Applications to five financial return series illustrate differences between data-driven and model-based fractional price estimates. The results support sequence-based learning as a computationally efficient complement to statistical inference under the assumed fractional model; they do not establish out-of-distribution accuracy or accuracy against observed traded-option prices.

title: The Defense Rests: A Courtroom-Inspired Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Automated Safety Case Generation
summary: Safety cases are widely used to demonstrate that mission-critical systems, such as autonomous vehicles and unmanned aerial systems, can operate safely after deployment. However, manually constructing safety cases is complex, time-consuming, and labor-intensive, which calls for the proposal of automated approaches to support their creation. Inspired by the legal nature of safety case construction, we formalize the safety case creation problem through a courtroom analogy, where stakeholders collaboratively propose, examine, criticize, review, improve and validate safety claims and their supporting evidence. In this analogy, the safety analyst acts as a prosecutor by identifying hazards and safety concerns, while the assurance case developer serves as a defense attorney by constructing and substantiating safety arguments. An orchestrator acts as a judge by coordinating stakeholder interactions, and a review board serves as a jury by assessing argument completeness and persuasiveness. Based on this formalization, we propose eTrustWare, a Large Language Model (LLM)-based multi-agent framework for automated safety case generation and review. Our experiments on several safety cases of ML-enabled autonomous driving systems demonstrate the feasibility of coordinated LLM-based agents for generating safety cases.

title: Grid-Aware Assessment of Forced Oscillations from Spatially Distributed Large Loads
summary: This paper develops a unified analytical framework for assessing forced oscillations induced by spatially distributed large-load fluctuations to determine their grid-aware fluctuation magnitudes. Emerging computational loads, such as hyperscale datacenters, present cyclic power variations with dynamic impacts depending on the waveform characteristics, forcing frequency, and source location. Our grid-aware framework represents these fluctuations using deterministic harmonic and probabilistic spectral models, and analyzes the resulting bus-wise frequency deviations based on a generic grid frequency-response model. Deterministic, risk-aware, and band-based probabilistic severity measures are further developed to obtain admissible fluctuation limits under different assumptions on frequency and phase uncertainty. We also formulate a security-constrained (SC) optimization of locational fluctuation magnitudes among existing large loads, accounting for their aggregated frequency deviation level. Case studies on the IEEE 39-bus and 14-generator Australian systems validate the proposed severity measures and admissible limit analysis. The SC optimization results further show that distributing a given amount of aggregate fluctuation toward dynamically less sensitive locations can substantially reduce system-wide oscillation severity.

title: Locally Linear Generalized Single Index Regression
summary: In this work we propose and analyze a procedure for estimating a generalized single-index regression model. This generalized single-index regression framework models the conditional mean of the responses $Y$ as a function of the covariates $X$ where the mapping is assumed to have the form $f \circ g$, where $g$ is $β$-Hölder with $β\geq 2$ and $f$ can be a discontinuous function of bounded variation. We propose a general procedure that operates under minimal assumptions about the distribution of covariates $X$, requiring only boundedness, sufficient smoothness and absolute continuity with respect to Lebesgue. Our procedure jointly estimates the gradient vector $\hat v(x) \approx \nabla g(x)$ and the conditional mean $μ(x) = f(g(x))$ by solving a localized weighted linear least squares problem. We derive central limit theorems for gradient vector estimates $\hat{v}_x$ and regression estimates $\hatμ(x)$, and we derive rates of convergence for our approach, illustrating that it indeed achieves a stochastic convergence rate matching the minimax mean squared error rate when $β= 2$ and $f$ has a locally Lipschitz derivative. Unlike prior approaches our velocity estimation results accommodate link functions in the local bounded-variation class, allowing for nonsmooth and even discontinuous links while retaining consistency and asymptotic normality at almost every inference point. Finally, we instantiate this model in the situation where $g = Π$ is a closest point projection onto a compact and regular embedded $C^3$ curve $γ$, a setting recently studied in the literature. We also supplement our theoretical results with experiments on real and synthetic data to demonstrate the utility of our procedure.

title: Stochastic Modeling of the Mean Time Between Software Failures: A review
summary: A review of several models for the software failure detection stochastic process is per- formed. We focus on how the Mean Time Between Failures is obtained from those models and present a comparative study. The models considered involve some of the well known based on non- homogeneous Poisson processes and a recently proposed model based on contagion. Our main target is to evaluate the models performance when they are applied to modern software projects developed under Agile methodologies. Recently developed Software Engineering practices (TDD, Scrum, etc.), propose an iterative procedure be- tween development, testing and debugging, introducing this way, particular challenges to Software Reliability modeling. As opposed to the non-homogeneous Poisson processes, the failure rate of the contagion model depends not just on time but also on the number of previously detected failures. All the considered models are particular cases of non- homogeneous Birth Processes, a general fundamental theory on how to obtain time to failure and time between failures expectations is also shown.

title: FM-Mamba: An Efficient Native 2D Selective State Space Model with Stability-Aware Discretization
summary: When applied to two-dimensional features such as images, Mamba-based methods either flatten the feature map into 1D sequences and fuse multiple scans, which breaks spatial adjacency and multiplies computation, or recurse directly on the 2D grid but rescale the recurrence with a fixed input-independent factor and aggregate only the predecessors on a single anti-diagonal, leaving the discrete step unconstrained by 2D stability theory. We propose \textbf{FM-Mamba}, a native 2D selective state space model built on the general Fornasini--Marchesini (FM) model. Its coupled recurrence evolves along both spatial axes; cross-axis coupling induces a discrete diagonal-predecessor term $\tilde A_0$, and two independent input-dependent step sizes $Δ_1(i,j)$, $Δ_2(i,j)$ govern propagation along the two axes, so that the coefficients adapt per position and per direction. A normalized ratio $r_k=a_{0,k}/(a_{1,k}a_{2,k})$ yields a closed-form piecewise bound on the two step sizes; when a configuration falls outside the stable interval the steps are projected onto this bound, and the criterion is re-verified per position after training, which suppresses systematic local amplification without global damping. The recurrence is executed by a dual-diagonal wavefront scan: each update gathers information from two anti-diagonals, and the input enters the current state through a single projection, so that neither training nor inference flattens the feature map. Code is available at https://github.com/BitSsm/FM-Mamba-Runtime

title: A mechanistic characterization of missingness at random
comment: 70 pages: 34-page main text followed by 36-page supplement
summary:
The missingness-at-random (MAR) assumption underlying many missing-data methods describes abstract statistical independences, whereas practitioners reason more naturally about the causal mechanisms that generate missingness. To bridge this gap, we provide a mechanistic characterization of MAR in terms of paths in a directed acyclic graph (DAG) modified to allow certain edges to cease to operate when an incomplete variable is missing, a property termed "context-specific causal irrelevance (CSCI)". Under a faithfulness condition, MAR holds if and only if the modified DAG contains no MAR-violating paths. Without CSCI, this condition reduces to a previously established d-separation condition, VMAR; thus, MAR without VMAR requires specific kinds of CSCI, as can occur with monotone dropout. These results shift the burden on investigators from passively invoking MAR to justifying, on substantive grounds, the specific mechanisms it requires.
  We then consider identification of a target law p(v) of variables V by a MAR-assuming analysis, e.g., multiple imputation, that includes complete auxiliary variables Z (variables not in V). Barring a perfect cancellation, such an analysis recovers p(v) if and only if MAR holds with respect to V and Z jointly. We show that if there exists any set of auxiliaries such that (V, Z) obeys MAR, then the complete candidate auxiliaries that are ancestors of the target variables or their missingness indicators form a sufficient set. Contrary to standard recommendations, not all candidate auxiliaries should be used: even complete auxiliaries can introduce MAR violations that would not otherwise occur.
  We illustrate these results with simulations and an analysis of sexual identity change in the Stockholm Public Health Cohort, where our results indicate that a candidate auxiliary, income, should be excluded; including it attenuated estimates toward the null.

title: From AIOps Pipelines to Agentic Service Operations: A Survey of Capability, Authority, and Evidence
summary: Modern service systems combine rapidly changing dependencies, heterogeneous telemetry, and operational actions whose side effects may amplify an incident. Conventional AIOps research has produced effective detectors, localizers, and diagnostic models, yet surveys typically organize them by task, telemetry modality, or learning technique. Such taxonomies describe what a method predicts, but not which decisions it may make or which evidence justifies that authority. We survey the transition from AIOps pipelines to agentic service operations through three coupled lenses: capability, operational authority, and evaluation evidence. We first relate SOA, microservices, Kubernetes, service meshes, and serverless platforms to the incident lifecycle. We then review conventional AIOps methods and audit 22 language-model-enabled systems according to their evaluated behavior rather than their intended autonomy. The audit shows that most systems remain copilots or read-only investigators. Only two exercise write authority; both use constrained action envelopes, and neither carries controlled production-outcome evidence. Building on these findings, we synthesize a four-plane reference architecture, evidence grades, an evaluation ladder, and a controlled adoption path. Together, these artifacts clarify which claims current evaluations support and what evidence is still required for dependable agentic service operations.

title: Facet-offset Polytope Expansion for Dynamic Operating Envelopes of Aggregated Distribution Grid Resources
comment: 2027 IEEE PES Grid Edge Technologies Conference & Exposition
summary: This paper presented a facet-offset polytope expansion framework with sensitivity-informed directions (FOPE-sen) for constructing DOEs in three-phase unbalanced distribution systems. The facet directions are selected from DGR coordinate directions and sensitivity-informed network-critical directions, while the facet locations are determined through a two-step bisection procedure guided by a power-flow feasibility oracle. Numerical results demonstrate that FOPE-sen captures at least 106% more flexibility per dimension than box-shaped and random-direction expansion methods. Moreover, FOPE-sen constructs DOEs comparable to or larger than those of VBPE while using fewer than 1/40 as many facets in dimensions greater than four. Future work will focus on stronger safety verification for nonconvex AC feasible regions, scalability in high-dimensional spaces, and extensions to multi-aggregator allocation and market-participation applications.

title: COSI: A Framework for Robustly Valid Inference
comment: Slides based on this paper can be found at https://arun-kuchibhotla.github.io/docs/talk/ (These slides includes more examples and sometime more simulations. The discussion in some of these slides is also informal.)
summary: We introduce COSI (COnfidence from Scale Invariance), a framework for constructing confidence sets for statistical functionals. COSI builds on the HulC (Hull-based Confidence), which uses median unbiasedness to construct confidence sets from batch estimates. COSI uses scale-invariance properties shared by many common estimators. We divide the data into batches, compute an estimate in each batch, and retain each candidate parameter value for which the batch estimates pass a test of scale invariance. The resulting confidence sets are asymptotically valid under weaker assumptions than classical Wald and bootstrap procedures require, and their coverage can be closer to the nominal level in small samples. Applications include robust inference for the mean, regression coefficients in misspecified linear models, tensor norms, and Fréchet means.

title: On Improving the Adoption, Usability, and Retention of Static Application Security Testing (SAST) Tools
comment: 56 pages, 8 figures. M.S. thesis in Cybersecurity, Montana State University
summary: As the Internet connects more of the world, software vulnerabilities create growing security risks. Because software developers are responsible for building and maintaining secure applications, they rely on tools and techniques that help identify vulnerabilities early in development. Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tools analyze source code to identify potential security weaknesses before software is deployed. Although SAST can help developers address vulnerabilities proactively, these tools also present usability and adoption challenges. This thesis examines those challenges and explores ways to improve the adoption, usability, and continued use of SAST. First, a literature review of 89 research works related to SAST implementation and continued usage identifies recurring developer concerns, including false positives and other usability barriers that can reduce trust in SAST results. Second, the thesis presents a process for automating the execution of SAST tools and formatting their output so that findings are more meaningful and actionable to developers. A real-world use case evaluates an implementation of this process and gathers developer feedback. Participants reported satisfaction with several aspects of the process and indicated that it increased their willingness to use the SAST tool.

title: Semantic Communication via Analog RF Computing: When the Radio Computes the Meaning
summary: Semantic communication (SC) systems transmit continuous latent representations of meaning, but computing the semantic encoder at resource-constrained edge devices incurs substantial energy and memory costs. To address this challenge, we propose an end-to-end SC framework that executes the semantic encoder in the client's RF receiver front end using analog RF computing. A base station (BS) broadcasts encoder weights as RF waveforms, while each edge device reuses its receiver's passive mixer to compute semantic latents at ultra-low energy. These latents are transmitted over the uplink for network-side task inference. We show that analog computing noise across encoder layers and channel noise affecting transmitted latents admit a unified mathematical model. We define a task-posterior semantic distortion metric and derive its second-order decomposition into per-client, per-stage semantic sensitivities. Using this decomposition, we obtain a closed-form semantic-aware water-filling allocation of the total client energy budget across clients, encoder layers, and uplinks, assigning tighter accuracy targets to semantically sensitive stages. This allocation induces a broadcast beamforming problem that accounts for client-specific, per-layer accuracy requirements. We further refine the allocation through stochastic optimization and jointly design it with multi-task noise-aware training of the shared semantic model. MNIST simulations show that, at matched total client energy, the proposed allocation reduces network semantic distortion by 9.2\%-19.2\% compared with uniform precision and 5.1\%-13.1\% compared with client-blind allocation. Noise-aware co-design yields a further 46\% reduction.

title: Bandit Online Submodular Minimisation Using Zeroth-Order Oracles
summary: We consider online submodular minimisation under bandit feedback, where at each round a decision maker plays a subset and observes only its cost, while the cost functions, and hence their minimiser, change over time. Existing bandit methods only guarantee static regret, which compares against a single fixed subset and is a weak benchmark when the minimiser moves. This paper provides, to the best of our knowledge, the first method with guarantees for tracking a moving minimiser in this setting. We propose a zeroth-order method built on a two-point oracle for the Lovász extension whose two evaluations are both subsets that can be played. The perturbed and base points are rounded by a common random threshold, and drawing the smoothing direction from the unit sphere makes the base evaluation a zero-mean control variate, so the oracle is an unbiased estimator of the smoothed gradient. We establish dynamic regret bounds of order $O\big((1+\sqrt{P^\ast_N})N^{3/4}\big)$ in general and $O\big((1+\sqrt{P^\ast_N})N^{2/3}\big)$ under a sufficiently small drift, where $P^\ast_N$ is the path length of the minimiser sequence, together with the corresponding $O(N^{3/4})$ and $O(N^{2/3})$ static regret bounds. Numerically, the method attains lower regret than the algorithm of (Hazan and Kale (2012)), with the advantage growing with the path length.

title: CrisisBench: an evaluation suite for crisis counseling AI
summary:
Background: Crisis helplines are essential to mental health systems but are often understaffed and underfunded. LLMs could support counselors, but existing benchmarks do not capture the escalation, risk assessment, and de-escalation central to crisis conversations, while privacy restrictions limit use of real transcripts.
Methods: We present CrisisBench, a privacy-preserving suite for single- and multi-turn crisis counseling evaluation. It includes 1,085 single-turn tasks from 200 de-identified conversations and 1,185 patient LLMs derived from hotline metadata. Patient models and a 23-item LLM judge were calibrated against expert counselors.
Results: We evaluated five GPT models plus draft-then-edit and retrieval-augmented generation. All systems underperformed human counselors on excessive empathy and questioning in single-turn evaluation. The rubric achieved human-human Krippendorff's $α$ = 0.51 and LLM-human $α$ = 0.54 (Pearson r = 0.80). In multi-turn evaluation, retrieval-augmented generation scored highest overall (0.961), with all systems within 0.058. Microskills and style/tone were near ceiling, while productivity and safety/risk accounted for most between-system variation. Counselors rated patient LLMs realistic (86%) and useful (92%).
Conclusion: CrisisBench enables scalable, privacy-preserving evaluation of crisis counseling. Current systems perform strongly on core structural competencies but still diverge from experts on important response-level failure modes. We release the rubrics, judge prompts, and evaluation tasks.

title: Stability-Constrained Imitation Learning for Performance-Guaranteed Neural Feedback Frequency Control in Microgrids
summary: Guaranteeing performance for frequency control is challenging within traditional control paradigms, as it demands precise disturbance estimation and real-time control signal computation within a timeframe of seconds. This paper addresses this challenge by proposing a stability-certified imitation learning framework for frequency regulation in low-inertia microgrids. Based on the frequency response model of the microgrid, an offline numerical optimal control is employed to generate near-optimal pairs of state and control dataset, which are subsequently used to train a deep neural network (DNN) feedback controller. To ensure the closed-loop stability, the DNN controller is trained with a set of Lyapunov-based stability constraints derived using absolute stability theory. Such an imitation learning paradigm can significantly improve the training efficiency, while the resulting DNN controller acts as an end-to-end function that simultaneously handles disturbance estimation and control optimization. The proposed framework is validated on a modified IEEE 33-node diesel-wind microgrid. The DNN controllers are deployed in wind turbine generators (WTGs) to provide decentralized, intelligent supplementary active power support to always maintain frequency deviations within predefined safety bounds under different disturbances while preserving closed-loop stability.

title: Deep Mixture Models: A Statistical Review with R
summary: Deep mixture models extend finite mixture models through hierarchical latent factor structures with shared mixture parameters. This focused review examines deep Gaussian mixture models (DGMMs), robust deep mixture models (RDMMs), deep skew-$t$ mixture models (DStMMs), and mixed deep Gaussian mixture models (MDGMMs) within a common statistical framework. We compare their pathway distributions, measurement models, and latent architectures, highlighting the implications for likelihood evaluation and inference. For continuous measurements, we discuss Gaussian conditional calculations and the scale-mixture methods underlying Student-$t$ and skew-$t$ pathways. For mixed measurements, we consider response-specific likelihoods and numerical integration for discrete variables. Alongside the review, we introduce \texttt{MixedDeepMM}, an R package providing a unified interface for fitting and evaluating deep mixture models with Gaussian, Student-$t$, and skew-$t$ kernels, supporting continuous and mixed measurements and single- and two-head architectures. We illustrate its use on the UCI Wine and Cryotherapy datasets, reporting clustering measures with standard errors across repeated fits and visualising consensus partitions. For mixed data, Gower silhouette widths complement external clustering agreement measures. We conclude by discussing computational challenges, model selection, and uncertainty assessment.

title: The Software Engineering Factory: Engineering Accountability and Control in the Age of Abundant Code
comment: Manuscript submitted to the "New Frontiers in Software Engineering" track of ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology (TOSEM)
summary:
AI agents can now plan, write, test, review, and revise code at a volume no human organization can inspect line by line. Final code review therefore cannot remain the primary organizational control for owning code changes.
  The Software Engineering (SE) Factory moves control into the process that produces the code. The Factory protocols define how work moves, what evidence must exist before it can proceed, and who owns the result. A deterministic protocol engine, implemented in conventional code rather than prompts, enforces those protocols by controlling stage transitions, requiring evidence, and invoking gates and human escalation, where needed, before work can advance. The SE Factory preserves human authority over consequential decisions and makes accountable acceptance possible without requiring humans to supervise every agent action.
  The SE Factory is not a dark factory. Humans remain in control by defining the scope and granularity of delegation, the boundaries and escalation conditions, and the consequential decisions that require accountable human judgment.
  We draw on our experience building three distinct SE Factory implementations, all of which have undergone multiple iterations and two of which are publicly available as open-source systems, into ten principles for conceiving, building, and operating SE Factories at scale, grounded in the organizational and technical realities of our implementations. We do not claim that these principles are exhaustive or constitute the only viable foundation for an SE Factory. Rather, we offer them as a conceptual scaffold and shared vocabulary for reasoning about SE Factories, evaluating their designs, and guiding their evolution. Our goal is to catalyze a community-wide dialogue that moves software engineering beyond controls designed for human-scale code production toward a disciplined, scalable, and trustworthy agentic future.

title: AI Agents Executing an RMS and EMT Ride-Through Workflow on a 2,000-Bus Synthetic Texas Grid: A Case Study with Open-Source Tools
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Submitted to the 2027 IEEE PES General Meeting
summary: This paper reports a case study of engineer-supervised AI agents executing a predefined RMS and EMT ride-through workflow on the 2,000-bus ACTIVSg2000 synthetic Texas grid with open-source tools. The test case is a 133 MW battery with a co-located 130 MW data-center load, assessed against ride-through criteria fixed before simulation and for loss of synchronism elsewhere in the grid. One agent ran 44 RMS cases and 15 without-project comparisons in ANDES; the other ran a 220-row EMT intake bench and an 84-row system study in DPsim and ParaEMT on a Kron-reduced area. Across the 44 RMS cases, 127 criterion cells fail, including loss of synchronism in all 44. Two findings concern the project plant. The battery keeps absorbing reactive power during sags on the light-load schedule (B3, as low as -19.8 Mvar on S4 T1), and the data-center load returns only at 5.00-5.56 s after long bolted faults (L3), which misses the ERCOT load-return requirement. In 13 of the 15 comparisons, which the authors selected after slips or speed-gate stops, the same machines slip without the project; the other 29 runs have no without-project comparison. RMS and EMT values differ in network, plant model, controls, operating point, and base, and so they are reported as separate, unaligned observations. The paper reports the errors the authors identified in the agent logs, 63 author messages, and 3.8 days from agent start to the integrated study report. The agents executed and documented the predefined ride-through and stability workflow, which covers one part of an interconnection study.

title: Training Neural Networks to be Locally Adaptive
summary: Deep neural networks fitted by global empirical risk minimization commit to a single model for the entire covariate space. In a regression problem, if the regression function $f_0$ is inhomogeneous --- varying rapidly in one region, while being nearly flat in another --- no single model can be appropriate everywhere, and the fit degrades where the function varies most rapidly. Here we study an alternative in which, instead of fitting the network globally, we fit it locally. For each query point $x$, a \emph{local neural network} is trained on the $k$ nearest-neighbours of $x$ alone, making the training sample and the fitted function query-dependent. We analyze the performance of the resulting estimator through a localization approach, establishing that the pointwise risk of the estimator with an appropriate choice of $k$ attains the rate $n^{-2α/(2α+d^{*})}$, up to logarithmic factors, when $f_0$ is locally $α$-Hölder with $α\in(0,1]$ and the covariates are supported on a $d^{*}$-dimensional manifold embedded in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$. A matching Le Cam lower bound shows that this rate is pointwise minimax optimal. However, the local rate-optimality requires $k$ to be calibrated to the smoothness of $f_0$, which is unknown in practice. We therefore provide a locally adaptive choice of $k$ that makes the neural network adapt to the local Hölder exponent of $f_0$ and to the intrinsic dimension simultaneously, both of which are potentially varying over the covariate domain. An extensive simulation study demonstrates the dominance of the locally adaptive neural network over a globally trained network and several state-of-the-art methods.

title: Trustworthy AI Teammates for Software Engineering: A Research Agenda for Lifecycle Context, Explainability, and Agentic Collaboration
comment: Accepted at the 2026 Pan-African Artificial Intelligence and Smart Systems Conference (PA-AI&SS 2026)
summary: Large Language Models are rapidly changing software engineering (SE) practice by supporting code generation, testing, debugging, documentation, and program comprehension. Yet most current AI coding assistants remain reactive tools: they respond to local prompts, rely on limited context, and provide suggestions whose rationale is often difficult for developers to inspect. This paper argues that the next phase of AI-assisted SE requires a shift from coding assistants to trustworthy AI teammates. We present a research agenda for human-AI co-evolution in SE, organized around three requirements. First, AI systems must become lifecycle-aware, reasoning across requirements and other deployment artifacts rather than isolated files or prompts. Second, they must provide principled explanations that expose assumptions, evidence, trade-offs, and risks in ways that support developer judgment. Third, they must enable agentic collaboration, in which specialized AI agents participate in software workflows while preserving human oversight and accountability. We propose an evaluation framework that moves beyond isolated functional correctness toward collaborative quality, including contextual alignment, trust calibration, maintenance recovery cost, and traceability. We conclude by outlining open challenges for designing AI systems that improve software quality without weakening human understanding, agency, or responsibility.

title: Benchmarking a Grid Foundation Model for AC Optimal Power Flow: Feasibility and Warm-Start Results on Synthetic Texas and South Carolina Grids
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the 2027 IEEE PES General Meeting
summary: Learning-based surrogates for alternating-current optimal power flow (AC-OPF) are often judged by the gap between their objective value and that of a nonlinear solver, which does not show that a prediction satisfies power balance and network limits. This paper tests whether predictions from the pretrained foundation model GridSFM-Open 1.1.0, recently released by Microsoft, are feasible AC-OPF operating points and whether they are useful initial values for a nonlinear solver. The model was evaluated zero-shot and after fine-tuning on 10, 100, and 1,000 labeled scenarios (FT10, FT100, and FT1000) on 500 scenarios for each of two synthetic grids, ACTIVSg2000 (Texas) and ACTIVSg500 (South Carolina), with Ipopt, MATPOWER MIPS, and pandapower PIPS as solver references. The lowest Texas median cost gap, 0.44\% for FT100, coincided with thermal violations in 24.1\% of cases and a median maximum bus power mismatch of 89 MW and 197 Mvar. Texas zero-shot predictions had a median maximum mismatch of 648 MW and 1,641 Mvar, and every South Carolina case violated a thermal limit for every model variant. Seeding Ipopt with FT1000 predictions gave geometric-mean solve-time speedups of 1.55x on South Carolina and 1.12x on Texas (p = 0.06, not significant at the 5\% level), while zero-shot seeds slowed South Carolina solves (0.26x). A small objective gap therefore did not indicate feasibility: although median zero-shot inference took only 1.32 s on Texas and 0.157 s on South Carolina on a shared host, every prediction still required a nonlinear solver, and fine-tuned predictions gave modest, grid-dependent warm-start speedups while zero-shot predictions slowed convergence on one grid. GridSFM may therefore be useful for initializing a nonlinear solver, but obtaining feasible AC-OPF solutions still required the solver.

title: Residual Curvature and Wald Calibration in Autocorrelation-Based Timescale Estimation
comment: 20 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. Reproducibility data and code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24283730
summary: Autocorrelation-based timescale estimation often fits a single exponential to a finite sample autocorrelation vector, even when the underlying process is not autoregressive of order one. We examine the first-order uncertainty of this fixed-lag projection under model misspecification. Standard extremum-estimation arguments yield a sandwich variance whose denominator is the full population curvature, including a residual-second-derivative term omitted by a Gauss-Newton approximation. A conditional sign rule and two stationary Gaussian examples with exact standard-error ratios 14/13 and 13/15 show that omission can underestimate or overestimate uncertainty. Full-to-Gauss-Newton population standard-error ratios are 1.34 and 1.45 in two K=36 noise-mixture models and range from 0.38 to 1.37 across an evaluated published-process parameter grid. In a follow-up experiment with 24,000 synthetic series, empirical standard deviations in four Gaussian models are consistent with the full-curvature scale at the main sample length, whereas the Gauss-Newton scale is substantially too small in the two noise-mixture models. In all 4,000 observed replicates of the primary condition, full-curvature intervals contained their Gauss-Newton counterparts, constraining the observed coverage gain to be nonnegative. Fixed-bandwidth HAC targets a smoothed long-run variance, and full sample curvature can worsen finite-sample coverage in an exactly specified model. Bandwidth-specific results, directional coverage errors, and oracle comparisons separate curvature effects from long-run variance estimation and transformation effects. These findings identify an application-specific discrepancy in a published autocorrelation-domain variance formula and characterize its asymptotic and finite-sample consequences.

title: Evaluating AST-Derived Knowledge Graph Retrieval for AIOps Incident Diagnosis in Apache Kafka
summary: Incident diagnosis requires retrieving source-linked operational evidence from large codebases. We evaluate graph-augmented retrieval for Apache Kafka using an abstract-syntax-tree (AST)-derived ownership graph over 1,600 source-linked log records and an audited benchmark of 315 incident-style queries covering 103 unique targets. Vector-only retrieval is a strong baseline at Recall@20 of 0.956, and neither static nor confidence-guided staged AST expansion significantly improves Recall@20 over it. As an external control we evaluate HippoRAG, a published text-derived graph-retrieval system, against its own ColBERTv2 retrieval backbone. Against ColBERTv2-only (Recall@20 0.803), HippoRAG attained 0.308; a post-hoc document-ensemble sensitivity raised Recall@20 to 0.648 but did not eliminate the deficit. Relative to static expansion, staging reduces cross-encoder pair workload and measured reranking time by about 52%. A manually evaluated 100-query downstream study finds no significant root-cause-correctness advantage for AST-derived structural evidence.

title: Device-Centric Cooperative Floor-Level Estimation under Sparse Anchor Deployment for Construction-Site Applications
summary: For construction-site applications in multi-story buildings, accurate floor-level estimation is important for tracking workers, equipment, and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. In buildings under construction, communication infrastructure and power-supply facilities are often limited and the indoor environment changes as construction progresses, making localization systems that rely on dense wireless infrastructure or fingerprint databases difficult to deploy and maintain. Low-power wide-area (LPWA) communication can provide wide-area coverage with a small number of temporarily deployed access points (APs), but under sparse AP deployment, AP-to-terminal observations alone may provide insufficient floor-related information for reliable floor-level estimation. To address this problem, this paper develops a device-centric cooperative floor-level estimation method that exploits inter-terminal observations as relative floor-difference information to complement AP-side information. For practical application with limited measurement data, AP-to-terminal observations are represented by an upper/lower-AP RSS contrast, while inter-terminal observations are statistically modeled according to floor-difference classes. The resulting AP-side and pairwise scores are combined in a weighted floor-label objective and approximately optimized using dual-order sequential iterated conditional modes (ICM). Ray-tracing simulations and LoRa measurement experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method under different AP deployments and terminal-selection limits.

title: Small Area Causal Inference
summary: We develop a framework for small area causal inference (SACI). Unlike the traditional doubly robust (DR) estimation approach, the new framework is based on the empirical best prediction (EBP) method. EBP takes into consideration not only the bias but also the variance factor, which is often a more dominant component in the mean squared prediction error (MSPE). Under a linear mixed model for SACI, we establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator of the model parameters. More relevant to our main objective, we establish asymptotic optimality of the EBP in terms of minimizing the MSPE of the area-specific causal-effect (ASCE) predictor. Moreover, in view of the traditional interest in causal inference, we establish asymptotic normality of the EBP of the ASCE , which is used to construct prediction intervals for the ASCEs. We carry out extensive simulation studies to investigate finite-sample performance of the proposed EBP and its comparison with the traditional DR and other existing methods. Our simulation results show that the proposed EBP method has significant advantage over the comparing methods in terms of MSPE and coverage probability and length of the resulting prediction interval. A real-data example from agricultural-animal genetics is discussed.

title: X-LocVul: An Evidence-Propagation Audit of Cascaded C/C++ Vulnerability Detection, Localization, and Explanation
comment: Full-length preprint: 21 pages, 13 tables, and 1 figure. Reproducibility artifact and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22723493
summary:
Developer-facing vulnerability analysis should link a function-level warning to a source location and a supported explanation. Cascaded systems can propagate weak evidence despite plausible components. We present X-LocVul, a measurement-first audit of a modular C/C++ detector-localizer-explainer pipeline combining UniXCoder, CodeT5, and Qwen2.5-Coder. We test whether evidence passed across stages is useful, merely source-resident, or misleading.
  Under duplication and temporal-leakage controls, UniXCoder has higher point estimates than CodeBERT, but true-CWE supervision is statistically indistinguishable from a shuffled-CWE control on PR-AUC, MCC, and vulnerable-class F1. Raw generated statements fail exact source matching in 90.83% of cases. Fuzzy projection reaches 83.79% Top-1 accuracy and exceeds semantic projection by 1.59 percentage points, although its advantage over raw ranking is not established. In a randomized, condition-label-masked two-rater evaluation of 50 paired cases, a predicted line improves evidence support, whereas a predicted CWE improves no endpoint. Oracle evidence improves evidence support (Holm-adjusted p=0.00453) and CWE consistency (p=3.49 x 10^-7), but not root-cause quality after correction (p=0.250); unsupported claims remain common. A chronological stress test retains ranking signal (ROC-AUC 0.782; PR-AUC 0.110), while the transferred threshold yields zero recall and F1.
  The contribution is not a state-of-the-art claim, but an auditable account of evidence construction, transfer, and consumption. It separates source residency from localization correctness, auxiliary labels from semantic supervision, and predicted evidence from useful evidence. Public E4 scores regenerate all 15 tests; missing manifests, final prompts, and profiler logs bound stronger reproducibility claims.

title: Grid-Responsive Pricing of Dynamic Wireless Charging with Coupled Residential Demand
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures. Submitted to the IEEE Power & Energy Society General Meeting (PESGM) 2027
summary: Dynamic wireless charging (DWC) is an emerging technology that enables electric vehicles (EVs) to recharge while traveling. Its unique operational model creates two revenue streams for DWC operators through lane access tolls and electricity sales. However, these prices influence not only traffic flow and roadway energy delivery but also how much EV charging moves to homes instead, potentially within the same distribution network. Neglecting this coupling can underestimate grid loading and compromise pricing decisions. We develop a coupled traffic, EV energy, driver-response, and AC distribution network model with a model predictive control (MPC) framework that jointly optimizes DWC tolls and charging prices while explicitly accounting for displaced residential charging and network losses. Using 78 days of I-210 West traffic data, we show that conventional MPC exceeds feeder loading limits on 52 days, whereas the proposed residential load aware controller eliminates these violations with only 0.6% lower operator revenue. Under a more constrained feeder configuration, it eliminates 50 overloaded days with a 0.9% revenue reduction. Sensitivity analyses highlight the importance of accurate residential demand estimation and feeder loss modeling, while peak-aware pricing further reduces daily peak loading by 3.7% relative to the base load. These results demonstrate the value of coordinated pricing that captures the interaction between roadway and residential charging.

title: Finite-Smoothing Efficiency and Inference in Single-Index Models
summary: When the error is independent of the predictors, its distribution can carry information about a single-index direction beyond the conditional mean. We develop Single-Index Kernel Density Regression (SI-KDR): at each candidate direction, it refits the link and evaluates a leave-one-out kernel log-likelihood of the residuals. Under Gaussian design, the population score vanishes at the true line at every positive smoothing tuple. At a fixed positive-curvature tuple, the leading covariance in the sample expansion is the conditional-mean efficiency bound times $Λ/G$, where $G$ is the information gain from independence and $Λ$ is the variance inflation from smoothing.
