We derive $Λ$ by following each observation through link refitting, the dual role of its residual as evaluation point and kernel center, and training standardization. Case-weight covariance estimates guide tuning for point estimation. Tuning separately at each candidate gives an exact conditional $F$ test. When predictors outnumber observations, independent screening that retains the support preserves the covariance comparison and the exact test, and $G/Λ$ becomes the squared-noncentrality ratio of a retained-coordinate test relative to the conditional-mean oracle. In four non-Gaussian error distribution designs at $n=600$, covariance-trace tuning reduced direction risk by 56% to 74% relative to reference bandwidths, and score-inversion coverage was 93.8% to 96.6%.

title: Usage Patterns of Programming Languages and Tools: A Systematic Literature Review
summary: Technology and the popularity of languages and tools are rapidly evolving. Thus, it is important to constantly assess the most popular languages and tools used in industry, furthering the collaboration between research and the software industry. In this study, we use a systematic literature review and investigate 37 studies published between 2015 -- 2024, which explored the programming languages, IDEs and CI tools used in industry. We observed that Java is most often listed among the most popular languages, and there are limited studies that investigate specific IDE usage. Also, Travis CI and GitHub Actions are the most common CI tools identified as being top CI tools used in industry. Overall, evidence shows that there is a lack of research focused on popular languages and tools used in industry, largely as there are many limitations with the possible methodology approaches. For example, lack of access to closed-source projects and sampling biases are potential issues that limit our understanding of popular languages and tools used in industry. In this regard, there is a need for more recent studies into development tools used in industry, involving multiple research approaches, to balance the limitations of each approach.

title: Safely Mitigating Grid Imbalance: A Hybrid Distributional Wide-Margin Recourse Approach
summary: This paper proposes the Multi-Agent Distributional Wide-Margin Policy Gradient (MADWMPG) framework: a dual-policy hybrid imitation and safe reinforcement learning (IL-SRL) method designed for safely mitigating grid imbalance in multiphase active distribution networks with distributed soft open points (SOPs). The framework comprises a wide-margin constraint barrier recourse (WCBR) module that seeks the maximal separation of constraint-compliant and unsafe actions and learns to proactively suppress exploratory violations. The framework addresses operational volatility using a novel adaptation of noncrossing quantile regression (NQR) distributional critics that track the complete distribution of policy returns. The set of behavior and recourse policies integrates an instantaneous physics-based and differentiable action projection mechanism that generates SOP constraint-compliant actions without relying on active learning. Policy safety is made responsive using an enhancement of conventional experience replay, and the safety performance of the framework is supported by probabilistic bounds derived in the paper. The proposed framework was trained and tested on a modified multiphase IEEE 123-bus test feeder. Results demonstrate its superiority to conventional reinforcement learning and SRL methods and show that it is highly competitive against the nonlinear AC optimal power flow.

title: Distributional change point analysis: high dimensionality, nonstationary dependence, and computational constraints
summary: We study general distributional change point analysis for high-dimensional time series under nonstationary temporal dependence and limited computational resources. To mitigate noise accumulation from irrelevant coordinates and reduce the computational cost, we propose a sparse random projection procedure based on characteristic functions. We quantify the computational complexity of the random projections and show that the required number of projections grows polynomially with the ambient dimension. To accommodate nonstationary temporal dependence, a Gaussian multiplier bootstrap based on contrasts of local empirical characteristic functions is developed. We establish asymptotic false detection control and simultaneous guarantees for estimating the number and locations of multiple change points, with a near-parametric uniform localization rate up to logarithmic factors. A key technical innovation is a Gaussian approximation for high-dimensional multi-scale sparse time series, which is of independent interest. Simulation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed procedure in detecting and localizing distributional changes under various temporal dependence structures. An application to neural recordings further illustrates the practical utility of the proposed method in detecting diverse distributional changes in neural activity.

title: PDFa11yMut: Mutation-Based Evaluation of Automated PDF Accessibility Validators
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Research artifact: https://github.com/gaurijain21/pdfa11ymut
summary:
Automated validators are widely used to assess PDF accessibility, but their detection boundaries are difficult to measure without controlled ground truth. A validator-clean PDF may be free of the implemented machine-checkable failures, or it may contain accessibility-relevant structural defects that the validator does not detect. This paper introduces PDFa11yMut, a controlled mutation-based benchmark for evaluating automated PDF accessibility validators against independently verified PDF structure defects.
  We generated 23 verified mutants from five validator-clean golden PDFs using five mutation operators targeting reading order, omitted assistive structure, heading hierarchy, marked-content association, and internal marked-content sequence. Each generated mutant was independently verified at the PDF structure level and checked for parseability, page-count preservation, and absence of detected visual differences. We then evaluated the mutants with three validators: PAC, Adobe Acrobat Accessibility Checker, and veraPDF, with veraPDF run using the PDF/UA-1 profile.
  The validators detected a small and highly operator-specific subset of the verified mutants. PAC detected 4/23 mutants (17.4%), while Acrobat and veraPDF each detected 5/23 mutants (21.7%). All three validators detected every generated heading-hierarchy mutant. None detected the reading-order swap, omitted-structure, or internal MCID-order mutants. Acrobat and veraPDF also detected one marked-content association mutant that PAC missed. The practical implication is that a validator-clean result can coexist with verified, visually invisible structure defects that affect the assistive representation of a PDF.

title: Solver-Free and Cost-Aware Online Scheduling of AI Data Center Tasks
summary: AI data centers receive computing tasks continuously, whereas solver-based optimization takes time to run and electricity is priced per settlement period. This paper bridges this timing gap through a solver-free online optimization rule inspired by dual decomposition. The rule assigns each task a start period upon arrival to optimize energy cost subject to operational constraints, shifting flexible tasks toward low-price periods while keeping high-priority tasks on schedule. Simulations on the A100 GPU trace (3,456 GPUs, 1,343 tasks) show that the proposed rule keeps GPU and CPU use within capacity while scheduling tasks at low cost. Compared with a multi-timescale optimization benchmark, it achieves a lower cost and, because it needs no solver, much less computation time.

title: Multilevel Filtering on Manifolds with Light Schrödinger Bridges
summary: In this article we consider the filtering of partially observed diffusions when the observations, made at discrete times, are noiseless. Each observation then confines the hidden state to a manifold defined by the data, whose type, for instance a sphere or an affine subspace, may change from one observation time to the next. In practice, the filter is approximated by particle filters, which require the diffusion to be discretized in time. Multilevel Monte Carlo reduces the cost of this discretization only if the particle approximations at consecutive discretization levels stay close, which standard particle filters do not ensure. We develop a new particle filter based on light Schrödinger bridges, which works between changing manifolds and can be coupled across discretization levels. A key insight is that the previous state enters the light Schrödinger bridge only through a few features, so that the bridge only has to be fitted on the new manifold, regardless of the type of the previous one. We bound the bias of this particle filter and the gap between its approximations at consecutive levels, and show numerically, on spheres and on manifolds that change type, that this gap is much smaller than with standard multilevel particle filters, and that, with the cost of the fits included, a hybrid estimator that uses it at the fine levels reduces the cost at small tolerances.

title: Ethics Suppression in AI Development: A Comparative Case Study of Responsible AI Under Competitive Pressure
summary: This study explores the governance tensions among Google, OpenAI, Meta, and Microsoft, focusing on how competitive AI development can lead to the ethics suppression. The study aims to examine how ethical oversight loses practical influence even when responsible AI structures are formally in place, especially during rapid technological competition. Despite the rapid growth of responsible AI frameworks and ethical principles in the tech sector, there has been less focus on how these concerns are actually applied when pressure to deploy increases. This paper introduces the concept of ethics suppression in AI development, highlighting that while ethical oversight may exist on paper, its practical authority can diminish during decision-making. Using a comparative qualitative case study examining corporate governance documents, public statements, and reports on governance issues, we identify common issues such as reduced authority, a weakened ability to escalate concerns, urgency in deployment, and fragmented governance. Our findings indicate that heightened competition can weaken the influence of ethical oversight, even in organisations with established responsible AI practices. By differentiating ethics suppression from ethics washing, it offers a framework for organisations and policymakers to evaluate the effectiveness of ethical oversight in competitive AI development.

title: Optimal Energy and LLM Task Scheduling for Multiple Cloud Data Centers
summary: This paper studies coordinated Large Language Model (LLM) training-task scheduling and facility operation for geographically distributed cloud data centers (CDCs). The central question is how two scheduling flexibilities - cross-CDC task transfer and task reordering - affect service and economic outcomes when remote execution remains subject to compute, bandwidth, energy, and zone-temperature constraints. We formulate a mixed-integer optimization model that jointly determines task outcomes, heterogeneous-node assignment, execution timing, pre-execution data transfer, node activation, and facility operation. A deterministic 24-hour case study contains 3 CDCs, 15 heterogeneous graphics processing unit (GPU) nodes, 4 thermal zones per CDC, and 103 tasks. In this instance, enabling transfer increases net profit by 57.9% relative to the otherwise matched no-transfer variant and increases completed tasks from 76 to 103. The more restrictive no-transfer FIFO-prefix variant completes 14 tasks and yields negative profit. The proposed schedule transfers 39 tasks, achieves 70.3% node utilization, and maintains zone temperatures within 24°C-27°C. These fixed-instance results indicate that cross-CDC transfer and task-reordering flexibility can improve the modeled profit and task-completion outcomes under the studied conditions.

title: Anytime-valid inference for conditional hazard and survival functions with streaming data
summary: We consider the nonparametric estimation of the conditional hazard, cumulative hazard and survival functions of a time-to-event variable from streaming data subject to censoring, truncation, or a cure fraction. A time-to-event model is a map from the distribution of the latent variables to that of the observed ones. For a large class of models this map has an explicit inverse, and the conditional hazard is the ratio of the density of the exactly observed durations to an at-risk function. Both are estimated by one-pass learners, in which each observation contributes once and is never revised, such as recursive kernel, series and histogram estimators. Our main result is an asymptotic confidence band sequence for the conditional hazard at a fixed covariate value, uniform in time and in the sample size, which allows monitoring after a burn-in, and stopping at a data-dependent time. The band can shrink at the optimal uniform rate up to a logarithmic factor. Bands for the cumulative hazard and the survival function follow. In simulations, a fixed-sample band inspected repeatedly fails in about half of the streams, while the miscoverage of the recommended bands stays below, or close to, the nominal level.

title: Reusing Battle-tested Code: A Systematic Literature Review of Automated Software Transplantation
summary: Software reuse remains a fundamental challenge in software engineering, often caught between the security risks of external libraries and the reliability concerns of generative AI. Automated software transplantation offers a compelling alternative by enabling the direct extraction and integration, into new host systems, of battle-tested logic (code that has already survived the rigors of production, possibly over many years of extensive in-production use). This paper presents a systematic literature review to evaluate the current state-of-the-art and identify the remaining barriers preventing this technology from becoming a mainstream engineering practice. We identified 27 distinct automated software transplantation approaches. Our analysis reveals that while the adaptation of code is highly automated, significant bottlenecks remain in the manual prerequisite steps of organ location and test suite augmentation. We conclude with a research roadmap that suggests how these manual obstacles might be overcome, including the strategic use of Large Language Models to assist in identifying and verifying high-value, production-hardened logic for transplantation.

title: Virtual EMI Receiver Generation (VERGE) for Improved EMI Removal in MRI
summary: MRI is not designed to operate in the presence of EMI emitting electronic devices. To accomodate this, we propose VERGE which improves on previous EMI removal methods and can operate without external EMI sensors. VERGE estimates a reference coil non-linearly from all imaging and non-imaging coils by training a small per-scan convolutional neural net to generate a virtual coil. The virtual coil is then used with STRIDE, a reference-based EMI removal method. For single-source EMI contamination, VERGE performed similarly to the reference method. For multi-source dynamic EMI contamination, VERGE outperformed the comparison methods. Notably, VERGE with zero physical EMI sensors outperformed the comparison methods even with two physical EMI sensors. A non-linearly estimated virtual EMI coil improves reference-coil-based EMI removal under dynamic multi-source EMI, and enables effective EMI removal without physical EMI sensors or training data.

title: Bivariate Renyi Tsallis Divergence
summary: In this paper, a bivariate extension of the differential Renyi Tsallis divergence is introduced for comparing two absolutely continuous bivariate probability distributions. Fundamental properties of the proposed divergence are studied, including non negativity, pseudo additivity under component wise independence, and invariance under monotone and nonsingular linear transformations. Relationships with Renyi, Tsallis, alpha, Bhattacharyya, and Hellinger divergence measures are also established. A sensitivity analysis is performed to compare the Renyi, Tsallis and Renyi Tsallis divergences under the Marshall Olkin and Gumbel type bivariate exponential models, taking the magnitude of Kendall's rank correlation coefficient as a common scale for dependence. The proposed measure is further developed for bivariate order statistics, with particular emphasis on the joint distribution of the minimum and maximum order statistics for several lifetime distributions, including exponential, Weibull, Pareto, and Rayleigh models. When the underlying distributions are unknown, a nonparametric estimator is constructed using bivariate Gaussian kernel density estimators with plug in bandwidth selection. The proposed estimator is applied to a real life dataset and bootstrap resampling is used to assess estimation uncertainty. The results show the applicability of the proposed divergence for comparing bivariate distributions and indicate that its finite sample performance depends on the order parameter and the distributions being compared.

title: A Model-Driven Automation Pipeline for Building Operation
comment: Accepted for publication at the 27th International Conference on Product-Focused Software Process Improvement (PROFES 2026)
summary: Building Control Systems (BCS) engineering in the Architecture, Engineering, Construction & Operations (AECO) domain remains a complex, manual, and error-prone process, with fractured tools and manual commissioning causing design and built reality to diverge into a performance gap. We argue that a fully integrated and automated, tool-supported workflow spanning design, programming, and operation is feasible and can improve efficiency while reducing manual effort and configuration errors. Building on model-driven engineering, we present an automated process pipeline for modeling, programming, and auto-commissioning BCS. It uses two domain-specific modeling languages with tooling support to synthesize and deploy executable artifacts from platform-independent models, replacing a fractured, multi-stakeholder handoff process with a defined four-step workflow and improving consistency across the engineering lifecycle. Our evaluation reports notable efficiency gains, improved adaptability, moderate-to-high user acceptance, and good performance with solid scalability.

title: Hardware Impairment Parameter Estimation in Fluid Antenna Systems by Inverse Optimization
summary: In this paper, the problem of estimating the hardware impairment parameters of fluid antennas (FAs) in a multi-base station (BS) multi-user communication system is studied. The actual hardware coefficients are unknown, whereas the FA positions and transmit beamforming vectors adopted by the BSs are known. We first formulate a forward spectral efficiency (SE) maximization problem and introduce aggregate interference variables whose consistency with the physical inter-cell interference can be maintained through a pricing mechanism. For inverse estimation, the aggregate interference is obtained from receiver-side interference measurements associated with the observed network decisions. We then construct a trust-region linear model of the position-update problem around the observed FA positions. To extend the applicability of the proposed framework to antenna positions obtained from inexact or heuristic algorithms, we develop an inverse optimization model with an explicit duality-gap tolerance, which is solved using sequential quadratic programming (SQP). Simulation results show that the proposed scheme attains a lower estimation error than KKT residual minimization (KKT-RM) at both considered transmit-power levels and improves the SE by up to 22.86% over the Ideal-hardware-assumption scheme.

title: Online Inference for Dynamic Categorical Regression
summary: The multinomial probit is a widely used model for categorical data in many applications, especially in econometrics and the discrete-choice literature. The computational challenges encountered when fitting this model still motivate ongoing research from the frequentist and Bayesian viewpoints. We consider a dynamic formulation based on a state-space model, where at each time one observes a sample from a multinomial probit whose parameter evolves according to Markovian dynamics, thereby inducing dependence across time. We show that the filtering and predictive distributions of the latent parameter belong to the unified skew-normal family, developing an associated i.i.d.\ sampler to approximate quantities of interest via Monte Carlo. Motivated by the computational bottlenecks of the sampler encountered for larger sample sizes, we also develop approximate methods for online inference based on assumed density filtering and expectation propagation. This gives more scalable, yet accurate, algorithms for online inference about the latent state and prediction of future observations. Finally, we derive a novel expectation maximization procedure to learn from the data the covariance matrix underlying the latent-utility representation of the multinomial probit. We investigate the performance of the proposed methods on simulated data and on a real dataset of reservations from an online booking platform.

title: Fragmented Markers, Mixed Results: A Systematic Review of AI Coding Assistants and Developer Productivity
comment: Accepted at the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE '26)
summary:
AI coding assistants are increasingly embedded in software engineering practice, yet the literature still offers no cumulative, easily interpretable picture of their effects on software developer productivity. The central problem is not a lack of studies, but a lack of comparability: prior work operationalizes productivity through heterogeneous markers, settings, and reporting styles, making cross-study conclusions difficult. To address this, we conduct a staged systematic literature review. In the first stage, we synthesize studies that explicitly examine developer productivity. In the second, we extend the scope to productivity-related developer outcomes using SPACE as a theory-informed lens, capturing human-centered evidence that explicit productivity studies often omit. Across both stages, we analyze how productivity is operationalized, which confounding factors are discussed, and how reported effects are distributed.
  We identify 187 unique productivity and productivity-related markers, while individual studies typically only use five, revealing a broad but highly fragmented evidence base. Explicit productivity research is dominated by time-, output-, and artifact-oriented proxies, whereas the broader SPACE-aligned corpus makes satisfaction, psychological aspects, and well-being substantially more visible. Reported effects are often positive, but this pattern is stronger in perceived and tendency-based findings than in objective or statistically evaluated ones. Overall, the literature suggests that AI coding assistants can support productivity, but current evidence does not yet support simple, context-independent conclusions. The key contribution of this review is therefore a structured basis for making productivity evidence more interpretable, multidimensional, and comparable across studies.

title: Connections Between Instrumental Variable, Pseudo-Linear Regression, and Prediction Error Methods in Terms of Their Minimized Criteria
summary: This paper explores the connections between the criteria directly or indirectly minimized by Prediction Error (PE), Instrumental Variable (IV), and Pseudo-Linear Regression (PLR) algorithms for the identification of output-error models. By definition, PE methods aim to minimize the variance of the prediction error. In contrast, the correlation functions appearing in the stationarity conditions of IV and PLR algorithms are not the gradients of any underlying loss function involving a signal variance. Nevertheless, if the true system lies in the model set, we show that one IV algorithm minimizes asymptotically the variance of an unmeasurable signal called the equivalent prediction error. This signal was introduced previously to analyze the bias distribution of PLR schemes. It turns out that, regardless of whether the true system lies in the model set, some iterative IV and PLR algorithms aim to minimize the prediction error variance and can therefore be interpreted as indirect PE algorithms.

title: Randomization-Based Nonparanormal Adjusted Marginal Inference
summary: Adjusting for prognostic baseline covariates in the analysis of randomized controlled trials is recommended to increase the precision of treatment effect estimates. Such adjustment, however, introduces a complication known as noncollapsibility: for effect measures such as the log-odds or log-hazard ratio, the estimated treatment effect becomes conditional instead of marginal. Methods that target a marginal estimand even after covariate adjustment have been developed, but typically rely on population-based inference, which assumes patients are randomly sampled from some larger population, rarely true in practice. Such methods have been shown to inflate type I error, particularly in small samples or when many covariates are adjusted for. Inference based on randomization requires no such assumption, as it relies on the randomization scheme, which is known exactly, yielding a test that is exact even in finite samples. We present a randomization-based test for covariate-adjusted marginal treatment effects, built on nonparanormal adjusted marginal inference, applicable to continuous, binary, ordinal, and time-to-event outcomes. In simulation studies, this test controls type I error where the standard Wald test does not. Applied to 20 historical phase III time-to-event randomized trials, the covariate-adjusted estimator achieves precision gains comparable to an existing competitor method.

title: Measuring Human-AI Alignment as an Early Indicator for Effective Collaboration in Hybrid SE Teams
comment: Accepted at 1st International Workshop on LiveWriting @ ASE 2026
summary: As AI agents increasingly integrate into software engineering (SE) processes, ensuring effective collaboration in these hybrid teams becomes a critical challenge. While existing metrics focus on observing dynamic run-time performance, there is a lack of systematic, static measurements for early human-AI alignment -- the degree to which an AI's actions and granularity map to human expectations. This position paper proposes a research agenda to develop an SE-specific alignment metric suite drawing principles from software architecture, organizational psychology, and human-computer interaction. Furthermore, it outlines a validation methodology using concepts and techniques from business process monitoring (BPM) and introduces static assessment tools leveraging declarative BPM languages to ensure agents adhere to specific project constraints.

title: Data-driven model reduction: An identification perspective using Generalized Bases of Orthonormal Functions
summary: This paper proposes a data-driven model order reduction approach based on system identification concepts. A revised equation error formulation is introduced, in which the model is parameterized using Generalized Bases of Orthonormal Transfer Functions (GBOFs). The generalized reduction problem is formulated in the Hambo frequency domain associated with the GBOF transform. The frequency-domain fit of the reduced-order model is adjusted through the selection of the basis poles. A fit indicator depending on these poles is introduced, providing valuable heuristic guidance for their selection.

title: FAST: Functional Adaptive Sensing and Testing for Quickest Change Detection
summary: Quickest change detection (QCD) is studied for partially observed functional data streams. At each sampling epoch, a function is realized over a continuous domain, but its values can be observed at only a fixed number of locations. At an unknown change point, the functional mean undergoes a shift that is assumed to admit a sparse representation in a localized basis. We propose Functional Adaptive Sensing and Testing (FAST), which jointly estimates the unknown post-change parameter, selects sensing locations, and performs sequential detection. A minimax lower bound on the worst-case detection delay is derived under an average-run-length constraint. A non-asymptotic estimation-error bound is established for the policy-dependent observations induced by adaptive sensing. Under the stated regularity conditions, FAST is first-order asymptotically optimal when sensing subsets are optimized exactly. Simulations and a wildfire case study demonstrate the performance of the proposed procedure.

title: Trusting Trust in AI Software Engineering Agents: The Why, What, and How?
summary: AI software engineering agents are increasingly integrated into development workflows, from autocomplete assistants to autonomous repair agents and multi-agent software development pipelines. Trust matters because these agents can produce, revise, and pass on artifacts that developers, other agents, or organisations may later rely on under uncertainty and risk. Yet trust in such systems is often treated as a single measurable property of an AI system. This is insufficient for software engineering, where trust depends on who relies on the agent, how that reliance is structured, and which properties must hold in that deployment. We propose a structural framework for reasoning about trust in AI software engineering agents. Inspired by the recursive nature of trust in software systems, we decompose trust into three analytical questions: Why trust?, identifying the trust scenario; What trust?, identifying the trust configuration; and How much trust?, identifying the trust properties. From these questions, we derive three scenarios, four configurations, and five trust-relevant properties, state which of these are closed by construction and which remain open to revision, and instantiate the resulting profile on a ChatDev-style multi-agent workflow. The framework is conceptual, and is offered as a foundation for the empirical work that would validate it, rather than as a numerical trust metric.

title: Explicit Dual Model Predictive Path Integral Control
summary: In this work, we present a fully sampling-based explicit dual control algorithm that combines a particle filter and model predictive path integral control for partially observed nonlinear systems. The key idea is to roll out multiple sampled input sequences from all particles of the particle filter to obtain a belief-averaged control cost that induces caution. The same rollouts are used to sample imagined future measurements, which are drawn from the predictive distribution of the particle belief. This results in a Monte Carlo information term that gives a sample estimate of the expected information gain of each sampled input sequence and thereby induces probing. In contrast to existing explicit dual control schemes, the proposed scheme neither relies on gradients of the dynamics or measurement models nor requires a Gaussian belief. Furthermore, all computations can be parallelized across input sequences, particles, and imagined measurements, which makes the scheme amenable to real-time implementation on suitable hardware. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in a simulation example of a planar terrain-aided navigation task.

title: Exact and Approximate Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Multivariate Diffusions under High-Frequency Sampling
summary: We establish the asymptotic theory of the exact maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) for discretely observed multivariate ergodic diffusions under high-frequency, long-span sampling, solving an open problem posed by \citet{YCW2019} and \citet{Li2013}. The drift may grow linearly, and the volatility is bounded away from zero and either bounded or proportional to $1+|x|$. When the sampling interval decays polynomially, the exact MLE is consistent, asymptotically normal and efficient, with rates $\sqrt{nΔ_n}$ for drift and $\sqrt n$ for diffusion parameters. Under an additional condition on ergodic averages, and when the time span $nΔ_n$ also grows polynomially, its moments converge as well. The proof never analyzes the exact likelihood directly: it shows that a closed-form density expansion of sufficiently high order is uniformly accurate in relative terms at every observed transition, so that the two log-likelihoods differ by $o_P(1)$ uniformly in the parameter. The same argument yields accuracy conditions under which an approximate likelihood is asymptotically equivalent to the exact one; in particular, the approximate MLE of Yang, Chen and Wan converges to the true parameter. For the delta-expansion estimator of fixed order $K\ge1$, we derive the leading bias explicitly. It shows that $nΔ_n^{K+1}\to0$ cannot be weakened when the bias constant is nonzero, and that the bias falls on the drift parameters for even $K$ and on the diffusion parameters for odd $K$. Monte Carlo experiments confirm the predicted biases.

title: We Fixed the Scorer First, and Cluster Correction Killed Our Own Planted-Defect Result in AI Code Review
summary: Judging an AI code-review pipeline only by how much it catches hides an axis: what it dropped. Stronger selection raises precision for free; the cost never reaches the report. We ran four arms on the same eight cases, one scorer, asking whether planted-defect detection can rise without raising the claim error rate. Three repetitions are nested in eight cases, so p is reported per contrast and twice: under an exact permutation test over cases (2^8 arrangements) the two contrasts publishable under independence (Fisher p=0.017, 0.019) move to 0.0625 and 0.109, and after Holm correction no contrast separates. This is "not observable with this design," not "no effect": the sign test needs six discordant cases in one direction, its realized type-I rate under the null is 0.0078, and 80% power needs a per-case win probability near 0.80; closing it takes 12-25 cases, not repetitions. Within a run, a second pass never removes what the first found (0/24, 0/24 paired losses) while its gains (+3, +2) fall in one case; baselines on byte-identical prompts differed 15/24 vs 20/24, so run-to-run variance exceeds the effect. The claim error rate is 0.0% (0/178), with no upper bound on the rate claimed; scorer discrimination was measured with pre-registered positive controls (12/12 fabricated claims rejected, 0 false rejections). We retract our original causal explanation and report the instrument defects we hit. The contributions are not the numbers: (1) fixing the instrument before seeing results, then killing our own main effect with it; (2) the identity eps-hat = eps-hat(pi): a reported error rate is computed only on the subset a retention policy kept, silent about what was dropped, so it does not identify the quantity an irreversible gate needs; no improvement in the number promotes an automated verdict to publish, delete, or history-rewrite surfaces; a mechanized refusal enforces this.

title: Model Augmentation for thermo-mechanical hysteretic dynamics
summary: Accurate prediction of thermo-mechanical wafer deformation is essential for sub-nanometer overlay in extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography. Localized heating expands the wafer, while friction between the wafer and its supporting elastic pillars causes hysteresis. Modeling this is challenging because of the system's large scale, the computational cost of friction-induced hysteresis and the sparse deformation measurements. This work augments a linear thermo-mechanical baseline model with a learning-based structure in a linear fractional representation (LFR) framework, identified from sparse measurements. Simulation results show that the augmented model captures the unmodeled dynamics with hysteretic effects and predicts the deformation significantly more accurately than the baseline.

title: TRAIL-IRL: Crossed Reward-Temperature Mixtures for Unlabeled Trajectory Clustering
summary: Different paths need not imply different preferences, trajectories also differ in how randomly actions are chosen. Many multi-reward inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) methods assume common action randomness and can confound it with preference heterogeneity. We introduce TRAIL-IRL, which clusters unlabeled trajectories using rewards for preferences and temperatures for action randomness. Its crossed mixture pairs each reward with a shared set of temperature levels, allowing action regularity to vary within preference groups. With centered and normalized rewards in a known finite-state environment, we establish the identifiability conditions under which the distribution of sufficiently long trajectories determines rewards, temperatures, mixing weights, and class counts up to relabeling. Under the same conditions and reward constraints, common-temperature reward mixtures with the same component count cannot reproduce a crossed mixture with multiple temperatures. We develop a generalized expectation-maximization algorithm and select class counts using the Bayesian information criterion (BIC). Simulations show improved predictive fit, reward recovery, and trajectory classification over common-temperature mixtures with the same component count. For 140 bird-year trajectories from 79 white storks, BIC favors four reward classes and three temperature levels over common-temperature candidates. Younger birds have higher posterior membership probabilities for a southwestward migration class, whereas older birds have higher probabilities for a northern retention class. Within reward classes, higher temperatures are associated with more variable movement directions and positions farther ahead along the migration route, consistent with social information use and collective sensing.

title: A Survey of Modeling Languages for Automotive Digital Twins
summary: The demand for digital twins and suitable modeling techniques in the automotive industry is increasing rapidly. Yet, there is no common understanding of digital twins in automotive, nor are there modeling techniques established to create automotive digital twins. Recent studies on digital twins focus on the analysis of the literature on digital twins for automotive or in general and, thus, neglect the industrial perspective of automotive practitioners. To mitigate this gap between scientific literature and the industrial perspective, we conducted a questionnaire survey among experts in the German automotive industry to identify (i) the desired purposes for and capabilities of digital twins, (ii) the modeling techniques related to engineering and operating digital twins across the phases of automotive development, and (iii) the role informal models play during automotive development. To this end, we contacted 189 members of the Software-Defined Car research project and received 96 responses. The results show that digital twins are considered most useful in the usage and support phase of automotive development, representing vehicles as-operated. Moreover, simulation models, source code, and business process models are currently considered the most important models to be integrated into a digital twin alongside the associated, established tools. Furthermore, informal models are frequently created digitally, e.g., using PowerPoint, mainly employed for communication and documentation during the conception and development phase.

title: MARS: Feature-guided physics-informed deep learning for real-time battery health and lifetime prediction
comment: 14 pages, 10 figures. Published in IEEE Transactions on Transportation Electrification, 2026
summary: Accurate and robust estimation of battery state-of-health (SOH) and remaining useful life (RUL) is essential for safe and cost-effective operation of electrified transportation systems, yet it remains challenging under operating variability, non-stationary aging, and non-Gaussian measurement disturbances. This paper proposes Multi-scale Adaptive Robust State Estimation (MARS), a multi-scale adaptive robust state-estimation framework that couples a dual-branch temporal encoder with an equivalent-circuit-model-constrained differentiable generalized-correntropy adaptive Kalman filter. The encoder disentangles fast intra-cycle voltage-current-temperature dynamics from slow inter-cycle degradation, and the fused degradation context adaptively parameterizes the cycle-level process covariance, measurement covariance, and correntropy bandwidth. Through the unrolled robust filtering recursion, MARS performs physics-consistent state propagation and generalized-correntropy-based innovation correction, while uncertainty decomposition and Monte Carlo dropout provide calibrated prediction intervals for SOH estimation and conditional RUL prediction. Experiments on the NASA and CALCE benchmarks demonstrate improved SOH accuracy, achieving mean absolute error/root mean square error values of 0.72%/0.92% and 0.63%/0.80%, respectively, together with competitive conditional RUL performance against representative data-driven and hybrid baselines. The resulting conditional-RUL prediction intervals achieve coverage probabilities of 100.00% and 99.24% on NASA and CALCE, respectively. Ablation, disturbance-sensitivity, near-end-of-life, and runtime analyses further verify the contribution of each module and the practical inference cost for online battery management.

title: Covariate-Indexed Inclusion Probabilities on Unbalanced Panels
summary: We estimate the probability that an item with given covariates belongs to a set when the cross-section changes over time and items and periods are dependent. We propose two convex models whose fitted probabilities are nonnegative by construction and remain valid whatever the dependence between items, for which we establish consistency, finite-sample bounds and limit distributions for serially dependent panels. One suits events of moderate or high probability, the other rare events, and half the disagreement between their fits estimates a lower bound on the misspecification error of the worse fit, without knowledge of the true probabilities. On monthly US stock failures, the rare-event model predicts better than the ordinary logit and the classical failure logit. With the eight classical predictors, most of the gain comes from basis functions of the rank angle of each predictor and summary.

title: Auditing Hyperstimulation at Scale in Child-Facing YouTube Videos
summary: Parents, pediatricians, and journalists have raised concern that child-facing videos are becoming increasingly overstimulating, but this concern rests mostly on ad hoc observation rather than systematic measurement. We present a large-scale audit of hyperstimulation patterns, which we refer to as content-independent production choices that may exceed young children's capacity to process comfortably. Drawing on parents' Reddit discussions and developmental psychology, we identify 12 hyperstimulation patterns and operationalize them as computational metrics. We apply these metrics to 16,375 videos from 542 child-facing YouTube channels spanning 2015-2026. We found broad increases in stimulation over time, with cut rates rising across all five content categories. Nearly a quarter of the channels increased in at least one stimulation pattern over time. More stimulating videos also tended to receive more views, but the relevant stimulation patterns differed across content types.

title: A Discrete Digital Isolator with Shielded Planar Transformer for Gate Driver Applications
summary: Galvanically isolated gate drivers are required in many power electronics applications. This paper describes an implementation of a digital isolator using discrete components with a planar coreless PCB signal transformer providing the isolation. The use of an electrostatic shield between the transformer windings is shown to provide sufficient common-mode transient immunity to support IGBT half-bridge drivers, an application subject to a severe dV/dt transient during switching. The design is verified through the experimental implementation of a prototype half bridge using two of the proposed discrete digital isolators with SiC power transistors and demonstrates common-mode transient immunity greater than 15 kV/us with very low implementation complexity.

title: Robust Actor-Critic Learning under Transport and Divergence Uncertainty
summary: Learning reliable control policies requires accounting for uncertainty in transition dynamics and errors introduced by function estimation and action generation. We develop an actor--critic method for discounted robust Markov decision processes with continuous states and actions and an unknown nominal transition law. We consider transition uncertainty sets defined by Wasserstein distance, total variation, Kullback--Leibler divergence, or Pearson chi-square divergence. A conditional diffusion model is fitted once to offline transitions. At each subsequent iteration, we estimate the robust action-value function from current-policy observations using a shared-target minimax criterion, then update a generative actor through exponentially weighted score matching. Regularization preserves exploration and provides the density regularity needed for conditional distribution estimation. Under coverage and regularity conditions, we establish finite-sample bounds for critic estimation, the learned conditional action law, and the robust return of the implemented policy. The bounds distinguish critic estimation error, uncertainty in the nominal transition model, and policy regularization, and characterize how the four robustness radii affect the resulting guarantees.

title: Can AI Help Explain AI? Effects of Multimodal LLM-Generated Explanations on Perceived Understanding and Perceived Trust in XAI Visualizations
summary: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) aims to make machine learning models understandable, yet many XAI visualizations remain difficult for end-users to interpret. Here, we evaluate whether augmenting XAI outputs with textual explanations from multimodal LLMs improves perceived understanding and perceived trust. We conducted a pre-registered within-subject experiment ($N = 128$) across seven decision scenarios and five XAI methods, with and without LLM generated explanations. The explanations improved perceived understanding and perceived trust by 0.35 and 0.26 points on five-point scales (both $p < .001$). The gain appeared in all seven scenarios, did not differ between local and global explanations, and was largest for participants with the least prior XAI exposure. A mediation analysis indicates an indirect effect on perceived trust through perceived understanding. These results suggest that multimodal LLMs can provide a useful interpretive layer for XAI beyond expert audiences.

title: Edge-Combining Subharmonic Mixer-First Receiver
summary: A 1-10 GHz subharmonic mixer-first receiver using edge combining to drive N-path switches from 50% duty-cycle clocks at half the local oscillator (LO) frequency avoids the gain penalty of harmonic mixing. Inverter-based differential baseband amplifiers with back-gate feedback linearization set their gain by process-defined capacitance ratios, using no additional components and consuming no additional power. A 22 nm fully depleted silicon on insulator (FD-SOI) prototype receiver achieves a conversion gain of 12.8-18.1 dB and a noise figure of 5.7-11 dB across the band. It achieves up to 15.4 dBm out-of-band IIP3 while consuming 16.7-22.3 mW.

title: Greedy Empirical Bayes for Density Estimation
summary: Bayesian nonparametric density estimation is challenging in high dimensions, where traditional approaches like the Dirichlet process (DP) mixture rely on computationally intensive Markov chain Monte Carlo or approximations. We introduce the partition posterior bootstrap (PPB), where a flexible prior is constructed by smoothing a DP over a partition of the sample space. Conditioned on this partition, exact posterior sampling reduces to a simple Bayesian bootstrap-like algorithm. Importantly, we select the partition using a greedy empirical Bayes (GEB) algorithm which scales to high dimensions and large sample sizes. GEB greedily maximizes the closed-form marginal likelihood via local split decisions arising naturally from its factorization, yielding an adaptive binary tree partition. Our key theoretical result is that the GEB tree belongs to an admissible family with high probability, splitting all identifiable signals while avoiding over-splitting noise. As a result, the PPB posterior with the GEB tree attains adaptive contraction rates. Our theory holds under weak, verifiable assumptions, which we demonstrate in numerous examples. Empirically, PPB delivers accurate density estimates and uncertainty quantification at a fraction of the computational cost of other approaches, making it a practical off-the-shelf choice for high-dimensional Bayesian density estimation with theoretical guarantees.

title: ClearTalk: Data-Driven Mandarin Articulation Analysis and Personalized Communication Support for Children with Dysarthria
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Accepted to the IEEE ICDM 2026 Teen Research Track
summary: Children with dysarthria may experience reduced intelligibility and difficulty expressing everyday needs. ClearTalk is a smartwatch-based system that converts Mandarin speech-recognition differences into interpretable articulatory profiles for personalized practice and staged communication. Target and recognized utterances are aligned at the syllable level, summarized across seven articulatory positions, and ranked by a count-sensitive asymmetric heuristic. For 13 dysarthric speakers from the Mandarin Dysarthria Speech Corpus, system syllable-level accuracy showed a Pearson correlation of 0.908 with expert intelligibility, with an R-squared value of 0.824 and a p-value below 0.001. The system-selected priority targets achieved an 86.7 percent overlap with the consensus of three blinded speech-language pathologists; across 210 target consonants, automated labels achieved 86.7 percent agreement, a Cohen's kappa of 0.76, and a macro-F1 score of 0.81. In a balanced single-session pilot with 15 children, mean pre/post gains were 14.4, 29.4, and 27.7 percentage points for mild, moderate, and severe groups, while communication-round completion rates were 81.3, 66.7, and 48.0 percent. These findings support the feasibility of using interpretable patterns of speech errors to guide wearable articulation practice and communication assistance.

title: Temporal Diffusion Models for Joint Signal-Channel Estimation under Gaussian and $α$-Stable MIMO Channels
summary: Diffusion models have emerged as powerful tools for learning complex data distributions and solving inverse problems. However, most diffusion models rely on the Gaussian distribution, which does not accurately represent heavy-tailed data. In this work, we study diffusion-based reconstruction under Gaussian and symmetric $α$-stable fading channels, while also exploring the benefits of using possible temporal dependence in the channel. We consider two variants: pilot-based channel-only estimation and joint image-channel recovery for MIMO systems. Our approach is based on several standard and score-based diffusion models for both Gaussian and $α$-stable distributions. We refine these models by guiding the reverse diffusion process using the observation likelihood and show how a single trained diffusion model can be reused for the location-scale family of distributions without retraining. In blind MIMO recovery, separate diffusion models are used for the image and channel, and their estimates are combined through likelihood guidance. For each setting, we compare independent and temporal reconstruction, where information from previous observations is used to improve the estimation. We show that, under a time-dependent channel model, such a temporal reconstruction improves channel estimation and the quality of the reconstructed image. Finally, we show that, for the same heavy-tailed channel data, using an $α$-stable diffusion prior provides better channel estimation and image reconstruction than using a Gaussian diffusion prior.

title: Copula-Based Synthetic Data Generation: A Use-Inspired Perspective on Trade-offs
summary: The generation of synthetic data offers a promising way to address challenges related to data scarcity and privacy concerns. While many approaches have been developed, tabular synthetic data generation methods often require complex models and extensive training data, while lacking interpretability. In this work, we investigate versatile probabilistic approaches using copulas, and leverage in particular the Gaussian Mixture Copula Model, to model the joint distribution of multivariate data, with a main focus on moderate-dimensional data sets. Taking a use-inspired perspective, we examine key trade-offs inherent to synthetic data evaluation, spanning fidelity, utility, and privacy, and demonstrate that copula-based methods achieve a sound balance across all three dimensions while remaining interpretable and providing an explicit probabilistic model. We illustrate and highlight the potential benefits of the method on a test case focusing on systematic missing values in a cardiovascular risk calculator and develop specific evaluation metrics for this application.

title: Digital Qiang Garden: Artist Residency as Interface for Creativity Under Change
summary: This research presents Digital Qiang Garden, an artist-led residency situated in Qiang ethnic minority villages in western Sichuan, China, as a practice-based inquiry into creativity for change. Rather than framing creativity as a discrete outcome or individual agency, the project examines how creative practice unfolds through lived conditions under uncertainty. Drawing from three years of residency practice, the pictorial identifies four creative modes of praxis that repeatedly emerged through shared living, material engagement, and cross-media collaboration. Through annotated visuals and project-based case studies, we further trace how these modes generated eight interrelated layers of change, spanning artistic processes, social relations, cultural encounters, ecological awareness, organizational structures, and artists' longer-term trajectories. By framing an artist-led residency as a transferable structure, this work contributes to HCI and creativity research by foregrounding designed conditions, situated action, and relational processes through which change unfolds over time.

title: Least ln-cosh-based adaptive filtering algorithm for graph signal processing
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Electronic Systems
summary: Currently, an increasing number of irregular signals are being defined within graph structures. This paper proposes a Least ln-cosh-based Adaptive Filtering for Graph Signal Processing (GSP LLAF) algorithm for offline/online graph signal estimation under various non-Gaussian noise conditions. Compared to the recently proposed Graph Adaptive Least Mean p-th Power (GSP LMP) algorithm, GSP LLAF eliminates the need for prior knowledge of the noise characteristics. Simultaneously, GSP LLAF addresses the limitation in estimation accuracy encountered by the Sign Algorithm for Graph Signal Processing (GSP Sign) and the Graph Signal Processing algorithm based on the Generalized Maximum Correntropy Criterion (GSP GMCC). Furthermore, the algorithm features low computational complexity and fast execution speed. To achieve a balance between convergence speed and estimation accuracy, a variable step-size variant, the Modified Variable Step-Size Least ln-cosh-based Adaptive Filtering Algorithm for Graph Signal Processing (GSP MVSS-LLAF), is proposed. In estimation experiments involving both static and time-varying graph signals, the proposed GSP LLAF and GSP MVSS-LLAF algorithms demonstrate fast, stable, and robust graph signal estimation performance under various non-Gaussian noise conditions, including Bernoulli-Gaussian (BG) modeled impulse noise, as well as alpha-stable, Cauchy, and Laplace distributions.

title: Sequential Conditional Paired-Sample Testing with Applications to Online Monitoring
summary: We study sequential conditional paired-sample testing, where observations arrive over time and the goal is to continuously assess whether two conditional distributions are equal given a common set of covariates. This problem arises naturally in model monitoring, where distributional changes must be detected without a prespecified terminal sample size, and in online comparisons, where responses are compared conditional on subject-level characteristics. We propose SCPT, an anytime-valid testing procedure for conditional distributions based on sequentially constructed conditional kernel discrepancy statistics and test martingales. The proposed method is nonparametric and accommodates a broad class of data-generating processes beyond the i.i.d. setting. We establish time-uniform Type I error control and derive asymptotic power guarantees under suitable regularity conditions. We also develop several useful extensions to address different needs, including testing under broader dependence structures, comparisons involving multiple auxiliary streams, and conditional goodness-of-fit testing. Simulations and real-data experiments show that SCPT effectively detects conditional distributional differences in streaming data, demonstrating its practical utility in a wide range of real-world applications.

title: RAW: Refusal Aversion in the Wild, A Causal Measurement Method for Deployed LLMs
comment: Accepted to the EMNLP 2026 Industry Track. 26 pages incl. appendices, 8 figures, 11 tables. Code: https://github.com/Pashasan/raw-refusal-aversion-in-the-wild Data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22073974
summary: Deployed LLMs field hundreds of millions of conversations a day and refuse a non-trivial fraction of user requests, yet the user-side cost of refusal, whether users disengage and by how much, is unmeasured on any production model: a blind spot for the consumer-facing platforms built on them. A/B-testing refusal is ethically and operationally constrained on frontier-lab products and unavailable to third-party platforms deploying these models through a fixed API. We introduce RAW, a method that uses LLM stochasticity as a natural experiment: at near-identical prompts in any existing log, the same model sometimes refuses and sometimes does not, and that variation identifies the causal user-side effect of refusal. Applying the method to 15 deployed LLMs in LMSYS-Chat-1M and WildChat, with user-clustered inference, we find that for about half of the models we can measure precisely, a refusal costs 3 to 17 pp of subsequent re-engagement; the rest show no distinguishable effect, among them one deployment whose positive point estimate we trace to persistent users retrying the refused request. Our contribution is the measurement method, which runs on any deployed model from logs alone for about \$0.30 per 1,000 conversations. We release labels, moderation scores, prompt embeddings, and pipeline code.

title: Robust DOA Estimation for GNSS-like Signals Under Jamming: A Rotation-Enhanced SWN-MUSIC Approach
summary: In jamming environments, accurate direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimation for Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-like signals using antenna arrays is crucial for spoofing detection and subsequent countermeasures. However, estimation accuracy strongly depends on the incident direction of the signal of interest (SOI) under a given jamming and array configuration, with severe errors occurring in certain directions---a phenomenon whose physical mechanisms remain unclear. To address this gap, we identify two types of geometric ill-conditions between the array manifold and the jamming subspace, clarifying that certain directions suffer from inherently unfavorable observation geometry, which cannot be overcome by algorithmic refinement alone. Motivated by this insight, we introduce a paradigm namely rotational diversity, which treats the array attitude as a controllable sensing resource to actively reconfigure the observation geometry, thereby providing complementary perspectives in which the problematic directions can be accurately estimated. To implement this paradigm, we develop a Rotation-Enhanced Spatial Whitening and Normalized Multiple Signal Classification (SWN-MUSIC) framework, which performs independent DOA estimations across multiple rotation angles and selectively integrates reliable estimates. Simulation results demonstrate substantial improvement in accuracy in the directions that were poorly estimated under the fixed-array SWN-MUSIC, while maintaining performance in well-conditioned directions, thereby producing more robust DOA estimates.

title: Testing the Pareto law through a Stein-Laplace characterization
summary: A Stein--Laplace characterization yields two closed-form goodness-of-fit statistics for the Pareto type-I family with unknown shape and known lower endpoint. The signed integral statistic $T_n$ has a standard normal limit after studentization, but explicit non-Pareto alternatives show that it is not omnibus consistent. The integrated squared discrepancy $S_n$ yields a consistent test against every fixed non-Pareto alternative on the specified support with a finite, positive logarithmic moment. We derive the weighted chi-square null limit of $nS_n$ and give conditions for an asymptotically valid parametric-bootstrap and plug-in covariance-operator method. The latter uses Nyström eigenvalue approximation to avoid repeated sample generation and parameter estimation. A large Monte Carlo comparison study shows competitive performance relative to existing procedures in the literature. In the paired study, the two calibrations have similar empirical power, with slightly higher small-sample rejection rates for the bootstrap in some settings. In the timing experiment, covariance-operator calibration is approximately $28$--$37$ times faster at $n=200$. An exploratory threshold-sensitivity analysis of Danish fire-insurance losses illustrates the dependence of Pareto goodness-of-fit conclusions on the specified tail region.

title: RelicTouch: Exploring Fingertip Vibrotactile Feedback for Image Interpretation
comment: 7 pages, The 23rd IEEE International Conference on Ubiquitous Intelligence and Computing
summary: Vibrotactile feedback is often used to simulate material properties on interactive surfaces, but less is known about how it can help users interpret visual differences during touchscreen exploration. We present RelicTouch, a finger-worn system that converts image-derived features into movement-contingent vibration. Study 1 was a controlled within-subject experiment (n=20) examining how vibration intensity, stripe spacing, and finger configuration affected haptic--visual congruence and subjective clarity. Study 2 was an exploratory qualitative study with eight domain experts examining how users interpreted cues generated from luminance and edge variation during continuous image exploration. Results suggest that cue legibility was associated with distinguishable signal changes, movement-based comparison, and visual or task context. Single-finger exploration yielded higher subjective ratings, whereas multi-finger feedback showed possible value for coarse comparison across separated features. These findings provide initial design implications for vibrotactile image exploration beyond material-simulation-oriented rendering.

title: Personalized Causal Low-Bitrate Coded Speech Restoration with Speaker Embeddings
summary: Legacy low-bitrate speech codecs such as AMR-NB remain widely used in telephony, where they restrict speech bandwidth and degrade listening quality. Coded speech restoration (CSR) aims to restore the speech bandwidth while improving the overall quality of coded speech, but typically without adapting to different speakers. In this paper, we systematically investigate personalization for restoration of speech coded at low bitrates, using a causal, low-complexity Universal Bandwidth Extension Generative Adversarial Network (UBGAN) model as the basis. We propose two personalization methods based on speaker embeddings, which incur little additional computational cost at inference: (i) conditioning a single CSR model on speaker embeddings, and (ii) cluster-based model selection, where multiple personalized models are trained on clusters of acoustically similar speakers. Experiments are performed on AMR-NB coded speech at 4.75 kbps. Experimental results with disjoint seen- and unseen-speaker test sets show that cluster-based model selection does not consistently outperform the non-personalized UBGAN baseline, whereas embedding conditioning significantly improves ViSQOL and WB-PESQ scores for both seen and unseen speakers.

title: JALE: A new Python toolbox for coordinate-based neuroimaging meta-analysis using activation likelihood estimation
summary: Coordinate-based neuroimaging meta-analysis using activation likelihood estimation (ALE) is commonly used to synthesize reported results of functional or structural magnetic resonance imaging studies. We here present JALE, a new, open-source Python package for conducting ALE meta-analyses. Besides computing standard ALE main effects and contrast analyses, this toolbox implements several novel analytical approaches including new options for thresholding (threshold-free cluster enhancement statistics, significance threshold prediction) as well as sensitivity and cluster analyses that were only available as in-house scripts in the past. The purpose of this paper is to provide an integrated conceptual foundation of recent developments in the ALE meta-analysis framework, with a particular focus on novel methodological implementations that can be executed in a straightforward and standardized manner using the new JALE toolbox.

title: Sleep2Word: Peripheral-to-EEG Translation via Duration-Aware Wordization
summary: Estimating full-night electroencephalography (EEG) spectrograms from peripheral measurements could extend EEG-informed sleep analysis to recordings acquired without EEG. This task requires compact representations of signals with different temporal structures. We introduce Sleep2Word, a framework for translating respiration, electrocardiography (ECG), or photoplethysmography (PPG) into EEG spectrograms through duration-aware physiological words. Building on context-dependent chunking, Sleep2Word groups physiological embeddings into variable-duration chunks and jointly quantizes their content and duration into modality-specific wordbooks. A block-autoregressive translator then predicts target EEG word identities and occurrence-specific duration refinements within fixed-duration blocks. This design accommodates independent source and target wordbooks, limits temporal drift, and shortens the autoregressive decoding path. Trained on over 20K PSG cases across 9 datasets, Sleep2Word consistently outperforms existing spectrogram generation baselines in EEG spectrogram reconstruction, sleep staging, arousal detection, and survival prediction. Compressing full night sequences by up to 69.7%, the learned words yield a favorable accuracy-compute trade-off. Sleep event analysis further shows that the learned words capture physiologically plausible associations across modalities, suggesting their potential for interpretable cross-modal analysis.

title: Reference Coordinates, Output Perturbations, and Information Loss in EEG Decoding
comment: 45 pages including supplementary material; 5 figures in the main text. Data and code included as ancillary material
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) decoders can respond to reference changes that preserve all relative-potential information. We use established measurement-operator theory to distinguish coordinate sensitivity, additional output-channel perturbations, and electrode loss. Exact pseudoinverse alignment supplies a consistency control; measurement-operator canonicalization (MOC) denotes a graph-Tikhonov estimator. The broader evaluation covers three public motor-imagery datasets and four decoders. The primary EEGNet comparison on Cho2017 and PhysioNet uses three paired training seeds, three shared noise realizations, and six front ends, with identical CAR training inputs sharing checkpoints. At 10 dB output perturbation, MOC-minus-raw disagreement was -0.144 and -0.107, while balanced-accuracy differences were 0.044 and 0.050, respectively; these four contrasts passed the retained Holm correction. MOC also reduced disagreement relative to pseudoinversion across all three seeds in both cohorts. However, comparison with fixed graph smoothing after pseudoinversion did not establish an additional MOC benefit. Preserving zero reference rows changed raw disagreement by less than 0.001 in magnitude; inverse-method predictions were unchanged. For canonical front ends, cross-reference disagreement was close to the reference obtained from independent noise within the same operator. Controlled weak-mode reconstruction and equal-rank electrode masks exposed separate stability and information-loss effects. The results locate the complete-reference gains within spatial processing under the specified stress model, while requiring decoding accuracy alongside consistency to assess practical utility.

title: Symmetries of Counterfactuals: Identification and Testability of Counterfactual Maps from Covariate Heterogeneity
summary: In general, counterfactuals are not identified from data alone, because many causal models produce the same observed distributions but different counterfactuals. A common approach to circumvent this problem is to restrict the mechanism to a class in which it becomes unique, such as triangular monotone maps or optimal transport maps. However, whether the assumed class is correct is usually not examined. In this work, we study what the data can tell us when covariates are available that influence the outcome only through its latent cause. First, we characterise all counterfactual maps that are consistent with the data. They differ from the true map by a group of symmetries that preserve the conditional outcome distributions given the covariates. The more these distributions vary across covariate values, the smaller the group. Second, we show that for the classes above, consistency with the data is equivalent to a single conditional independence, which yields a test of the assumed class. We illustrate both results on synthetic data and on the ACTG 175 HIV trial.

title: MInfoVisQA: A Multilingual Benchmark for Information-Rich Visual Question Answering
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel in vision-language tasks; yet, whether they maintain consistent understanding of information-rich visuals (InfoVis) when the surface language changes remains unclear. To quantify this capability, we introduce MInfoVisQA, a parallel benchmark with 8,960 QA configurations derived from 128 seed instances across 24 languages. We construct seed-matched, language-parallel visuals and QA pairs by disentangling numerical-structural data from text and programmatically synchronizing translated labels. We evaluate 25 MLLMs under two settings: Language-Aligned QA (LQA, matching visual-text languages) and Cross-Language QA (XQA, fixed QA language with varying visual languages). The results show that aggregate accuracy masks substantial robustness gaps: two models with comparable mean LQA accuracy (80.4\%) exhibit performance spreads of 7.8 and 20.3 percentage points across languages. Moreover, all 25 models score lower with non-English visuals under fixed English QA, underscoring the need for cross-language sensitivity metrics.

title: Structured Design of Layered Sparse Unitary Space-Time Modulation for Integrated Noncoherent and Coherent MIMO Communications
summary: This work presents a novel structured constellation design based on unitary space-time modulation (USTM) for integrated noncoherent and coherent multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) communications. Information is encoded into the sparse space-time matrices through two layers: a noncoherent layer that distinguishes points on the Grassmann manifold (subspaces) and a coherent layer that distinguishes among the Stiefel representatives associated with each of those points (bases for the subspaces). We consider sequential decoding of the two layers to reduce computational complexity, while explicitly identifying the matrix structures that favor this decoding strategy. The proposed constellation builds on a previous structured Grassmannian signaling design, which has the remarkable property of producing space-time matrices with a single nonzero entry per row, while introducing a novel systematic design for the second layer corresponding to the Stiefel representatives. The design of the second layer preserves the sparsity of the first layer and significantly reduces the decoding computational complexity, while ensuring reliable performance under sequential decoding and enabling a simple yet effective bit labeling, as validated by numerical results in terms of bit error rate (BER) and symbol error rate (SER). Numerical results also show graceful performance degradation under channel correlation and, for limited coherence intervals where channel state information at the receiver (CSIR) can be estimated only imperfectly, improved performance compared with classical space-time block coding (STBC) schemes based on QAM and PSK.

authors: Marcos Vinicius Gualberto Barbosa da Silva
title: Milk yield responses to heat stress in tropical dairy cattle
summary:
Context: Rising temperatures and warm tropical nights threaten dairy productivity and resilience across tropical landscapes.
  Objective: This study characterises multi-scale interactions among thermal regimes, nighttime cooling, metabolic heat load, and crossbred genetics on daily milk yield in Brazilian dairy systems.
  Methods: A 24-year panel (2001--2024) of 788,528 test-day records from 87,809 Girolando (Holstein $\times$ Gyr) cows across 408 municipalities was linked to weather data. Two-way fixed effects, distributed lag, and piecewise threshold spline models were estimated across yield quartiles and crossbred fractions.
  Results: While aggregate summaries suggest stable yield up to a daily mean Temperature--Humidity Index (THI) of 76, production-stratified splines show high-yielding cows lose milk starting at THI 68 and accelerating above 76 ($-0.162$ kg animal$^{-1}$ d$^{-1}$ unit$^{-1}$, $p=0.0062$), whereas low-yielding cows remain unaffected ($p=0.81$). Distributed lag models reveal an immediate drop followed by a deeper trough four days later. Lack of nighttime relief ($\mathrm{THI}_{\min} \ge 68$) reduces yield by an extra 2.37 kg animal$^{-1}$ d$^{-1}$ ($p \le 0.001$) and causes an 8.6\% loss after seven warm nights, whereas wide diurnal amplitude buffers output by $+1.60$ kg animal$^{-1}$ d$^{-1}$. At comparable high yields ($\approx 31$ kg animal$^{-1}$ d$^{-1}$), intermediate crossbreds ($1/2$ and $5/8$ Holstein) sustain yield up to THI 76, whereas $7/8$ Holstein cows decline at THI 68.
  Conclusions: Tropical dairy adaptation requires continuous nighttime cooling for high-yielding cows combined with balanced Zebu--taurine crossbreeding.

title: Asking What Matters: Disagreement-Guided Ambiguity Detection for Interactive Text-to-SQL
summary: Interactive text-to-SQL requires an LLM agent not only to generate executable SQL, but also to decide which uncertainty to clarify within a limited interaction budget. However, current clarification policies have three limitations: (i) they target surface ambiguity without testing its SQL impact; (ii) they miss ambiguities implicit in schema routes or domain knowledge; and (iii) they spend limited turns on unfocused or redundant questions. These limitations expose a critical challenge: identifying SQL-impacting ambiguity before the intended SQL is known. In this paper, we propose DisGuAD, a Disagreement-Guided Ambiguity Detection framework that specializes clarification selection. DisGuAD treats disagreement among plausible SQL interpretations as direct evidence of which uncertainty matters to the final query. Specifically, it constructs a query-term inventory, elicits contrastive SQL interpretations through complementary probe families, compares their canonical SQL components, and attributes recurring differences to user-facing clarification targets. A lightweight prioritization and dialogue-state mechanism then selects one high-impact unresolved target for clarification. Experiments on BIRD-Interact Lite and Full with two LLM backbones demonstrate consistent improvements in task success and clarification quality. Compared with the original interaction policy, DisGuAD improves normalized Reward by 4.40--8.97 points and raises overall critical-ambiguity coverage from 48.62% to 82.75% and from 45.76% to 85.14%. Its clarification signals further improve two independently designed static text-to-SQL frameworks by up to 13.97 Reward points while keeping their SQL generators fixed. These results demonstrate that disagreement among plausible SQL queries provides actionable evidence for selecting clarification targets that matter to downstream generation.

title: Classical heat exchanger fouling-resistance laws as first-moment identities of additive stochastic deposition
summary: Heat-exchanger fouling is monitored through the fouling resistance, whose record is routinely fitted with the classical linear (Ebert--Panchal) or asymptotic (Kern--Seaton) law, and the shape of the fit is often taken as evidence of the underlying deposition or removal mechanism. We show that it cannot be. If the deposit grows by non-negative, statistically stationary increments, the mean fouling resistance is exactly linear without removal and exactly the Kern--Seaton asymptote under first-order removal, whatever the microscopic deposition law. Shear-driven erosion, per-element detachment, intermittent sloughing and saturation of the surface all give the same mean curve, so a fit identifies a net deposition rate and a relaxation time, and nothing else. Modelling the deposit as a Levy subordinator, we show where the missing information lies and what it costs to retrieve it from monitoring data. Removal mechanisms separate in the variance: sloughing leaves a plateau scatter that persists even for smooth deposition and can be read from a record that saturates. Deposition laws separate only in higher cumulants, which the measurement noise of a thermally reconstructed resistance attenuates; the record needed to distinguish them grows as the fourth power of the conductance error, which places it beyond reach at realistic measurement accuracy. For the time to reach a cleaning limit, the deposition law matters only near the threshold; farther away, the mean rate and its uncertainty dominate the prediction.
